articles.title_original: Hybrid effects of exfoliated boron nitride nanosheet and carbon-based additives on thermally conductive polypropylene nanocomposites
articles.title_en: Hybrid Graphene–Boron Nitride Fillers Improve Polypropylene Thermal Conductivity
articles.excerpt_original: Thermally conductive polymers are used in miniaturized electronic components across industries to dissipate heat, prevent overheating, and maintain device quality. In this work, hexagonal boron nitride was used as the main thermally conductive filler in polypropylene. A synergistic effect was achieved by introducing 1-D carbon nanotubes and 2-D graphene nanoplatelets. Different variations of these materials have resulted in improved thermally conductive nanocomposites. Exfoliated boron nitride nanosheets along with purified carbon nanotube-based polypropylene nanocomposites had the highest thermal conductivity and thermal diffusivity results (0.742 ± 0.007 W/mK and 0.412 ± 0.012 mm 2 /s, through-plane) with a 208.3 % improvement compared to pure polypropylene. Enhancements in the network structure were also observed in thermal camera images, which showed that the temperature of hybrid nanocomposites could rise from ∼28°C to 38.1°C in 4 minutes, while non-hybrid and pure nanocomposite samples reached ∼35.7°C and ∼34.6°C from ∼28°C at the same time, respectively. Morphological and physicochemical characterizations confirmed that hybrid nanocomposites had a modified bridging design, indicating an increase in the strength of the interconnections between fillers and the polymer network, as well as the presence of crystalline regions, which allowed phonons to pass through the pathway efficiently. The synergistic effect on the thermally conductive nanocomposites has promising results for electrically operating sustainable devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers combined graphene nanoplatelets and carbon nanotubes with exfoliated boron nitride in polypropylene, achieving a reported 208.3% improvement in through-plane thermal conductivity versus pure polypropylene. The findings support hybrid nanocomposites for heat dissipation in electrically operated devices.

articles.title_original: Acoustically driven motion of single molecules at hBN surfaces
articles.title_en: Acoustic Waves Enable Directional DNA Transport on hBN Surfaces
articles.excerpt_original: Developments in single-molecule imaging and sensing techniques have enabled direct observation of biomolecular dynamics at interfaces, which has important implications for the fields of membrane biophysics, nanofluidic sensing and transport. However, integrating active surface transport, localization and control over molecule motion remains challenging, limiting further progress in the realization of single-molecule devices. Here, we introduce an integrated surface acoustic wave (SAW)-hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) platform as a contactless actuation platform for directional transport of biomolecules over hBN surfaces. hBN provides an atomically flat surface on which DNA can be confined and still retain in-plane mobility, whereas SAW actuation enables active and guided transport without requiring specific electrical, dielectric or magnetic properties of the biomolecules. Trajectory- and jump-based analyses show that increasing the SAW power leads to higher displacement bias in the streaming direction, resulting in transport velocities along increasingly more linearized trajectories. We thus demonstrate that SAWs can induce tunable directional transport of DNA molecules confined on hBN surfaces, providing a new approach for the on-chip manipulation of biomolecules in nanofluidic systems. Our findings have important implications for the development of advanced single-molecule sequencing platforms and other technologies for biomolecular manipulation and analysis.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a surface acoustic wave–hexagonal boron nitride platform for contactless, tunable transport of DNA molecules. The approach could support on-chip single-molecule sequencing and nanofluidic biomolecular manipulation.

articles.title_original: Ultra-narrow-gate single-electron transistors based on crossed graphene nanoribbons
articles.title_en: Crossed graphene nanoribbons enable locally gated single-electron transistors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) are promising candidates for next-generation nanoelectronics owing to their width-dependent bandgaps and high carrier mobility. However, integrating ultra-narrow GNRs into well-defined device architectures with local electrostatic control remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate a dual-gate single-electron transistor (SET) device consisting of two spatially isolated, in-situ encapsulated GNRs grown within hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) flakes, where one GNR serves as the transport channel and the other as an ultra-narrow local top gate, enabling nanoscale electrostatic modulation. Room-temperature transport measurements show that the GNR channel operates as a field-effect transistor with an on/off ratio of ${\sim} 2 \times 10^{3}$ ∼ 2 × 10 3 and a subthreshold swing of 150 mV⋅dec −1 under back-gate control, while the GNR top gate provides comparable electrostatic control despite its much shorter gate length, validating its role as an efficient local gate. At 15 K, the device exhibits clear single-electron transport characteristics, including periodic Coulomb blockade (CB) oscillations and gate-tunable Coulomb diamonds. Upon tuning the gate voltages, the transport behavior evolves continuously from Coulomb blockade to Fabry–Pérot interference, revealing a crossover from localized charge transport to coherent interference governed by the locally modulated potential landscape. Our results establish in-situ encapsulated GNRs as a promising platform for carbon-based nanoelectronics and for exploring one-dimensional quantum transport in locally gated nanostructures.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated dual-gate single-electron transistors using two encapsulated graphene nanoribbons, achieving local electrostatic control and clear Coulomb blockade at 15 K. The devices also showed a crossover to Fabry–Pérot interference, highlighting potential for carbon-based nanoelectronics and one-dimensional quantum transport.

articles.title_original: Status and perspective on mechanical and protective properties of PVD MeSiN nitride nanocomposite coatings
articles.title_en: Review assesses PVD MeSiN nanocomposite coatings for extreme environments
articles.excerpt_original: MeSiN nanocomposite coatings have attracted growing interest due to their exceptional combination of high hardness, wear, and corrosion resistance. However, existing studies still lack a comprehensive analysis of their microstructural characteristics, performance metrics, and optimization strategies. This review critically examines recent advances in the fabrication techniques, structure–property relationships, and potential optimization strategies of MeSiN coatings. Depending on the silicon content, MeSiN systems exhibit three structural regimes: solid solution, nanocomposite, and amorphous structure. Among them, the nanocomposite configuration, comprising nanocrystalline MeN grains embedded within an amorphous SiN x matrix, offers the most balanced improvement in mechanical strength and environmental resistance (hardness 20 ~ 40 GPa, oxidation temperature 900 ~ 1000 °C). The effects of Si and the Si-based coating structure in mechanical strengthening as well as corrosion and oxidation protection are discussed in detail. Furthermore, optimization perspectives are proposed. Multicomponent coating and multilayer architecture collectively enhance thermal stability, mechanical strengthening, and corrosion performance. Remaining challenges include limited understanding of degradation mechanisms under complex service conditions, the need for improved interface engineering, and the implementation of data-driven design strategies. This study offers insights into the development of next-generation MeSiN coatings for extreme environments in aerospace, marine, and manufacturing applications.
articles.summary_en: An academic review examines how silicon content, microstructure, multilayer architectures, and multicomponent designs affect the hardness, wear, corrosion, oxidation, and thermal performance of PVD MeSiN coatings. The work identifies nanocrystalline MeN grains in an amorphous SiNₓ matrix as the most balanced structure and highlights interface engineering and degradation under complex service conditions as ongoing challenges.

articles.title_original: Atomic-Scale Engineering of Single-Layer hBN through Pd and Pt Decoration: A Density Functional Theory Study
articles.title_en: DFT Study Examines Pd and Pt Decoration of Single-Layer hBN
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Metallic seed layers and fabrication-induced defects can significantly influence the properties of two-dimensional electronic devices. We investigate their effects on the electronic properties of atomically thin single-layer hBN and single- and four-atom Pd- and Pt-decorated single-layer hBN models. Density functional theory is used to study the structural stability, charge transfer, polarization, electronic structure, work function, tunneling characteristics, optical response, hydrogen adsorption, and the effects of external electric fields. We find that the Pt-decorated one has stronger binding and a higher tunneling probability than the Pd-decorated one, whereas the latter induces a larger out-of-plane polarization. These results provide atomistic insights into how metallic adatoms and displaced N atoms following vacancy formation affect the electronic properties of atomically thin materials. Such quantitative understanding is important for establishing design guidelines for reliable nanoelectronic devices.
articles.summary_en: A density functional theory study evaluates how palladium and platinum atoms affect the structural, electronic, optical, tunneling, and hydrogen-adsorption properties of single-layer hexagonal boron nitride. Platinum shows stronger binding and higher tunneling probability, while palladium induces greater out-of-plane polarization, offering design guidance for nanoscale electronic devices.

articles.title_original: Electro-discharge coating of AA 6062 using h-BN–Cu composite electrodes: surface, crystallographic and tribological characteristics
articles.title_en: h-BN–Cu Electrodischarge Coating Improves AA6062 Wear Resistance
articles.excerpt_original: In this work, the surface modification of AA6062 alloy was investigated by using electro-discharge coating (EDC) with powder metallurgy-based h-BN–Cu composite electrodes with h-BN weight ratios of 70:30, 50:50 and 40:60. The effects of electrode composition, peak current and pulse-on-time on surface morphology, roughness, elemental transfer, phase constitution, crystallographic characteristics and tribological performance were evaluated. SEM and 3D optical profilometry showed composition- and parameter-dependent surface characteristics, with the lowest areal roughness (Sa) of about 2.5 µm achieved with the 50:50 electrode. EDS analysis showed an increase in boron content from 18.30 to 49.39 wt.% with increasing h-BN fraction. XRD showed reflections for h-BN and Cu. The 50:50 composition resulted in a compact coating, a crystallite size of 9.5 nm and a dislocation density of 38 × 10¹⁴ m−². EBSD showed a composition-dependent Cu texture intensity (3.870–4.793 MRD), a nearly constant h-BN texture, and strong grain-boundary misorientation peaks at 40°–50°. The 50:50 electrode also showed the lowest wear rate of 0.000246 mm³/N·m at 15 A and the lowest coefficient of friction of 0.233. The surface microhardness increased significantly from 87 HV for the uncoated alloy to 308 HV after coating.
articles.summary_en: Researchers evaluated electrodischarge coatings on AA6062 aluminum alloy using h-BN–Cu composite electrodes with varying compositions and process parameters. The optimal 50:50 electrode produced a compact, harder coating with reduced roughness, wear rate, and friction coefficient.

articles.title_original: The research progress on metal-two dimensional semiconductor Schottky barrier reduction methods: A review
articles.title_en: Review outlines strategies to reduce Schottky barriers in 2D semiconductor contacts
articles.excerpt_original: In recent years, two-dimensional (2D) layered materials have become the core carriers for outperforming traditional semiconductors and are driving the innovation of next-generation electronic devices due to their excellent optoelectronic and mechanical properties. However, the Schottky barrier formed at the interface between the metal electrode and the 2D semiconductor material hinders carrier injection, which is a core obstacle to realizing high-performance devices. This article systematically reviews the recent research progress in reducing the Schottky barrier at metal-2D semiconductor interfaces and achieves low-resistivity Ohmic contacts. This work explored in depth the mechanisms of work function mismatch, Fermi level pinning (FLP), metal-induced gap states (MIGS), disorder-induced gap states (DIGS) and the interaction of interface dipoles with the interface Schottky barrier. Four main barrier-reduction strategies were summarized: materials design engineering, doping of 2D semiconductors, contact geometry optimization, and interface-assisted processes. Besides, several specialized methods were also included, such as single-sided edge suspension, aerosol jet printing, and the insertion of sacrificial layers. Finally, an outlook on contact-resistance optimization strategies for 2D semiconductors and their large-scale applications are presented.
articles.summary_en: A review examines how Schottky barriers at metal–2D semiconductor interfaces limit carrier injection and device performance. It compares materials engineering, semiconductor doping, contact-geometry optimization, and interface-assisted methods for achieving lower-resistance Ohmic contacts and scalable applications.

articles.title_original: Controlled Component Segregation in Vapor-Deposited Organic Semiconductor Glass Mixtures
articles.title_en: Controlled Segregation in Vapor-Deposited Organic Semiconductor Glasses
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Multicomponent vapor-deposited organic glasses are essential in organic electronic applications, but achieving controlled component segregation at the nano/mesoscale remains a challenge, hindering the rational development of high-performance devices. In this study, we investigate binary organic semiconductor mixtures of TPD (N,N′-Bis(3-methylphenyl)-N,N′-diphenylbenzidine) and TCTA (Tris(4-carbazoyl-9-ylphenyl)amine). Despite being miscible in the bulk liquid state, the co-deposited glassy films of these two organic semiconductors exhibit a range of segregation behaviors, from homogeneous to clearly phase-separated structures. We employed differential scanning calorimetry and resonant soft X-ray scattering (RSoXS) to study the component segregation behavior and used the National Institute of Standards and Technology RSoXS Simulation Suite, paired with Atomic Force Microscopy, to interpret the energy-dependent RSoXS spectra. Our results indicate that component segregation in co-deposited TPD/TCTA films is due to a kinetically-arrested nucleation-and-growth mechanism, in contrast to the segregation mechanism of a previously reported TPD/DO37 (disperse orange 37) mixture which is strongly immiscible in bulk. This work provides a demonstration of tunable molecular aggregation in organic semiconductor glasses, enabling access to a continuum of morphologies from homogeneously mixed to segregated phases.
articles.summary_en: Researchers studied how TPD and TCTA organic semiconductor mixtures segregate during vapor deposition. They found that kinetically arrested nucleation and growth can tune film morphology from homogeneous mixing to phase separation, potentially supporting improved control of organic electronic materials.

articles.title_original: GaAs semiconductor opening switches grown by halide vapor phase epitaxy
articles.title_en: GaAs opening switches achieve 2.5 kV pulses at 4 MHz
articles.excerpt_original: Semiconductor opening switches (SOSs) are pulsed power components that enable high-power, high repetition rate switching with ns switching times, but require deep junctions that can be onerous to manufacture using diffusion methods. We demonstrate an 80 μm GaAs SOS diode with a ∼38 μm deep junction grown under 1 h by halide vapor phase epitaxy. Graded p-type doping was achieved using dimethylzinc, while the n-type background doping was utilized for the n-type side of the junction. The diode doping profile was characterized using electrochemical capacitance-voltage, and scanning Kelvin probe force microscopy was used to identify the shape and depth of the junction. Single and multiple diode stacks were processed and then characterized with a pulser circuit to evaluate their SOS performance. A six-diode stack generated a 2.5 kV pulse cutting off a peak current density of 6.8 kA/cm2. Circuit gain ranged from 6 to 11, decreasing with input bias. Rise time as low as 900 ps and repetition rates of 4 MHz were achieved. The choice of GaAs opens a new application space for SOS devices with narrow pulses and high repetition rates.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated GaAs semiconductor opening switches grown by halide vapor phase epitaxy, producing deep junctions in under an hour. A six-diode stack delivered 2.5 kV pulses with 900 ps rise times and 4 MHz repetition rates, indicating potential for high-power, high-repetition pulsed-power systems.

articles.title_original: Edge-state transport in gapped bilayer graphene
articles.title_en: Edge-State Transport Observed in Gapped Bilayer Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract We investigate the electronic transport in gapped bilayer graphene (gBLG) devices. For certain edge terminations—typically a combination of zigzag, armchair, and bearded types—we observe edge state conduction within the band gap, which is opened by a gate potential bias between the two layers. The edge states can generate a non-local resistance. Band structure calculations of gBLG nanoribbons corroborate the existence of the edge states, whose edge localization can be switched by tuning the electron energy. However, their existence strongly depends on the edge termination and does not originate from a topological bulk-boundary correspondence.
articles.summary_en: Researchers observed edge-state conduction within the band gap of gapped bilayer graphene devices under gate-induced bias. The effect depends strongly on edge termination and can produce non-local resistance, without arising from topological bulk-boundary correspondence.

articles.title_original: Geometry-Driven Ultrahigh Current Density Field Emission from Vertically Oriented MXene Film Edge Emitters
articles.title_en: Vertically Oriented MXene Films Enable Ultrahigh-Current Field Emission
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract MXenes are promising cold cathode materials owing to their high electrical conductivity, solution processability, and tunable surface terminations; however, realizing high-current-density field emission from MXene film emitters remains challenging because their planar two-dimensional geometry generally provides limited field concentration and restricts the number of field-activated emission sites. Here, we demonstrate a geometry-driven strategy to achieve high-current-density field emission from vertically oriented MXene film edge emitters. By systematically controlling the film height and inter-electrode gap, the optimized emitter achieves a current density of 5020 mA cm–2 at 1520 V, which is more than an order of magnitude higher than the values reported for previous MXene field emitters. Enhanced performance is not governed by the field enhancement factor alone. Instead, it is enabled by the balance between sufficient local field enhancement and a large effective emission area. Experimental Fowler–Nordheim analysis, emission pattern imaging, and the screening-corrected field-enhancement model indicate that excessive field concentration can promote edge-localized emission and reduce the effective emission area, whereas the optimized geometry enables distributed edge emission with improved stability. These findings establish edge-geometry engineering as a design principle for transforming two-dimensional MXene films into high-current-density cold cathodes for vacuum nanoelectronics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated vertically oriented MXene film edge emitters achieving 5020 mA cm⁻² at 1520 V. The study identifies optimized edge geometry—not field enhancement alone—as key to stable, distributed emission for vacuum nanoelectronics.

articles.title_original: Heterojunction Engineering for Boosted Interfacial Charge Separation: Intimate Face-to-Face 2D/2D SnWO4/BiOBr Z-Scheme Heterojunction for Photocatalytic Remediation
articles.title_en: 2D SnWO₄/BiOBr Heterojunction Boosts Photocatalytic Wastewater Remediation
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Constructing 2D/2D heterojunction is an effective strategy to suppress the recombination of photogenerated carriers and boost the photocatalytic performance of semiconductor photocatalysts. In this study, a 2D/2D direct Z-scheme SnWO 4 /BiOBr (SWO/BOB) heterojunction photocatalyst was successfully fabricated through a facile hydrothermal route. Intimate face-to-face interfacial contact between SnWO 4 nanosheets and BiOBr nanoplates was verified by multiple characterizations.The as-prepared SWO/BOB composite heterojunction photocatalysts exhibited enhanced photocatalytic activity over bare SnWO 4 and BiOBr. The optimized 50SWO/BOB sample presented the highest degradation performance. Its RhB degradation efficiency within 25 min was 2.41 and 2.95 times that of pure SnWO4 and BiOBr, respectively, while its CIP degradation efficiency in 60 min was 3.44 times and 1.27 times higher than SnWO 4 and BiOBr. The improved photocatalytic performance is mainly attributed to the unique structural advantages of the 2D/2D heterostructure, which broadens the light response range and accelerates interfacial charge transfer. Radical trapping tests confirmed that h⁺ was the primary reactive species, and ·O 2 ⁻ acted as a secondary active species in the photocatalytic pollutant degradation process of the 2D/2D heterostructure. A direct Z-scheme charge transfer mechanism was proposed based on band structure analysis and existing active species. This work provides a facile strategy for the design of high-efficiency bismuth-based 2D/2D photocatalysts and theoretical support for the remediation of refractory organic wastewater.
articles.summary_en: Researchers fabricated a face-to-face 2D/2D SnWO₄/BiOBr direct Z-scheme heterojunction using a hydrothermal method. The optimized composite improved rhodamine B and ciprofloxacin degradation rates versus the individual photocatalysts, supporting application in refractory organic wastewater treatment.

articles.title_original: Giant elastoresistance in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene
articles.title_en: Magic-Angle Bilayer Graphene Shows Giant Elastoresistance
articles.excerpt_original: Strongly correlated and topological phases in moiré materials are exquisitely sensitive to lattice geometry at both atomic and superlattice length scales. Twist angle, pressure, and strain directly modify the lattice and thus act as highly effective tuning parameters. Here, we examined electrical transport in twisted bilayer graphene subjected to continuous uniaxial strain. Near the magic angle (≈1.1°), devices exhibited a pronounced elastoresistance that depended on band filling and temperature, with a gauge factor more than two orders of magnitude larger than that of conventional metals. In selected doping regimes, the elastoresistance exhibited a Curie-Weiss-like temperature divergence. We discuss possible microscopic origins, including nematic fluctuations and enhanced electronic entropy from fluctuating isospin moments. Our work establishes uniaxial strain as a versatile probe of correlated physics in a moiré material.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report elastoresistance in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene with a gauge factor more than two orders of magnitude higher than conventional metals. The strong, doping- and temperature-dependent response highlights uniaxial strain as a sensitive probe of correlated and potentially nematic electronic states in moiré materials.

articles.title_original: Effects of Resistance Compensation on Laser-Induced Graphene Electrodes
articles.title_en: Resistance Compensation Improves Laser-Induced Graphene Electrochemical Sensors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Laser-induced graphene (LIG) offers a promising approach for fabricating low-cost, flexible, and disposable electrochemical sensors. However, the electrical resistance associated with thin conductive tracks and their connections can introduce substantial ohmic potential losses, compromising potential control and distorting electrochemical measurements. Here, we report a paper-based LIG electrochemical platform incorporating a four-terminal configuration designed to minimize resistance-related distortions through separate current-carrying and potential-sensing pathways. The electrodes were fabricated by direct CO2 laser scribing of Kraft paper, producing a porous, graphene-like carbon network characterized by scanning electron microscopy and Raman spectroscopy. The electrochemical effects of resistance compensation were systematically investigated using cyclic voltammetry and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy with ferricyanide/ferrocyanide, hexaammineruthenium, dopamine, and paracetamol. Resistance compensation substantially improved voltammetric peak definition and potential control, shifting the dopamine oxidation peak from 0.70 to 0.40 V and reducing the fitted uncompensated series resistance from 197 to 35 Ω for hexaammineruthenium. In contrast, the charge-transfer resistance remained nearly unchanged, indicating that the observed improvements primarily resulted from reduced ohmic distortions rather than changes in intrinsic electron-transfer kinetics. Under resistance-compensated conditions, the LIG electrodes enabled dopamine determination over 120–900 μmol L–1, with a detection limit of 29 μmol L–1, and paracetamol determination over 125–1660 μmol L–1, with a detection limit of 37 μmol L–1, using cyclic voltammetry. articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a four-terminal, paper-based laser-induced graphene platform that reduces ohmic distortion and improves electrochemical potential control. The compensated electrodes enabled dopamine and paracetamol detection by cyclic voltammetry, demonstrating improved performance for flexible disposable sensors.

articles.title_original: Lightweight MXene–B₄C–Polyimide Nanocomposite for Simultaneous Cosmic Radiation and Electromagnetic Interference Shielding in Aerospace Avionics
articles.title_en: Lightweight MXene–B₄C Nanocomposite Targets Dual Radiation and EMI Shielding
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract At cruise altitudes, atmospheric proton radiation and electromagnetic interference (EMI) jointly threaten the reliability of flight-critical avionics. Conventional protection strategies typically address these hazards separately through aluminum- or lead-based radiation barriers and conductive copper-mesh EMI shields, increasing enclosure mass, volume, and integration complexity. To address this limitation, we present a lightweight dual-function MXene (Ti₃C₂Tₓ)–B₄C–polyimide nanocomposite that combines proton attenuation and EMI shielding within a single conformal material system. The framework integrates SRIM/TRIM-guided compositional design, controlled nanocomposite fabrication, proton-beam testing, broadband EMI characterization, and aerospace-relevant environmental validation. SRIM/TRIM simulations show that a boron-rich composition of 31 at% achieves complete stopping of 50 MeV protons at approximately 36 mm bulk thickness, with electronic stopping dominating energy loss and negligible backscattering. Surface-functionalized B₄C nanoparticles (~ 45 nm) and exfoliated MXene nanosheets are incorporated through solution casting and vacuum-assisted filtration. At 20 wt% B₄C and 15 wt% MXene, the 36 mm composite achieves 100% proton attenuation, approximately fivefold higher than an aerospace-grade aluminum reference, and 54.7 dB EMI shielding across the X-band (8.2–12.4 GHz). Electrical conductivity reaches 2.1 × 10⁴ S/m, flexibility is retained to a 2 mm bend radius, and areal mass is reduced by ~ 81% relative to a 2.0 mm aluminum reference. Selected RTCA DO-160G-aligned tests confirm performance retention after 500 thermal cycles and 1,000 h humidity exposure. articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a flexible MXene–B₄C–polyimide nanocomposite for aerospace avionics that combines proton attenuation and electromagnetic-interference shielding. The reported material achieved 100% attenuation of 50 MeV protons, 54.7 dB X-band shielding, and an approximately 81% lower areal mass than an aluminum reference.

It has been shown that under traditional high-purity boron oxide synthesis conditions, a clear correlation between the residual intercalated water content and the OH groups content is impossible because of the need to control more than three intensive thermodynamic parameters at synthesis.

articles.title_original: SiC-BN composites with extreme thermal and environmental stability
articles.title_en: SiC–BN composites withstand extreme heat and oxidation
articles.excerpt_original: Ceramic materials that maintain structural integrity and resist thermal-shock under extreme conditions are critical for many applications. Here we show that spark plasma sintered composites containing equal weight fractions of hexagonal silicon carbide (6H-SiC) and boron nitride (h-BN) exhibit exceptional stability under extreme high-temperature oxidizing conditions and unusually stable temperature-independent thermal conductivity across a broad temperature range. Under high-velocity oxygen-fuel torch exposure in air, it withstands prolonged heating and thermal-cycling at surface temperatures reaching >1500 °C, whereas pure 6H-SiC and h-BN rapidly fractures or erodes. Microstructural evaluation shows the formation of a multi-phase surface silica layer that further protects the material from oxidation. Finite-element analysis heat-flux map shows that intrinsic porosity mitigates thermal stress, while ReaxFF molecular dynamics simulations reveal thermally driven interfacial reconstruction and the formation of a Si-N/C-B-rich bonding network, enhancing the interfacial cohesion at elevated temperatures. This lightweight, easily machinable ceramic composite will be a promising structural material in extreme environment applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report spark-plasma-sintered silicon carbide–boron nitride composites that resist thermal shock, oxidation and prolonged exposure above 1,500°C. articles.title_original: Development of a Cold Wall Reactor System for the Low‐Pressure Chemical Vapor Deposition of BN on SiC Fiber Tow
articles.title_en: Cold-Wall Reactor Enables BN Coating of SiC Fiber Tow
articles.excerpt_original: A device is developed to coat a SiC fiber tow with BN by low pressure chemical vapor deposition in a cold wall reactor. A motorized spool system is installed to feed the tow into the reactor in preparation for continuous processing in the future. In the present work, the system is used solely to control the mechanical tension of the tow, which is held stationary and heated by microwaves. The heating process induces a temperature gradient, with the temperature decreasing from the core to the surface of the multifilament tow. The precursor gas used is triethylamine borane mixed with ammonia. X‐Ray photoelectron spectrometry analyses demonstrate the feasibility of depositing a boron nitride coating with good purity. Key parameters include the preferred use of N 2 over H 2 as a carrier gas and a sufficiently large reactor diameter. Deposition growth rates are determined in situ by interferometry from non‐contact pyrometric measurements. Deposition kinetic regimes are identified as a function of temperature. The kinetics are limited by chemical reactions up to at least 1500 °C, before being limited by mass transfer and precursor depletion at the highest temperatures.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a cold-wall low-pressure CVD system for depositing high-purity boron nitride coatings on SiC fiber tow. The reactor incorporates motorized tow handling and identifies temperature-dependent deposition kinetics, supporting future continuous processing.

articles.title_original: Enhanced mechanical and thermal properties of OH-BNNS reinforced SA/PAM double-network hydrogels
articles.title_en: OH-BNNS Reinforcement Improves Mechanical and Thermal Performance of Double-Network Hydrogels
articles.excerpt_original: In this work, hydroxylated boron nitride nanosheets (OH-BNNS) reinforced sodium alginate/polyacrylamide (SA/PAM) double-network hydrogels were successfully prepared via free-radical polymerization and Ca2+ ionic crosslinking.The hydroxyl functionalization significantly improved the dispersibility of BN nanosheets in aqueous systems and promoted strong interfacial interactions with the polymer matrix. The incorporation of OH-BNNS and the formation of the SA/PAM double-network structure effectively enhanced the mechanical and thermal properties of the hydrogels. Compared with pure PAM hydrogel, the ternary composite hydrogel exhibited a tensile strength of 106.36 kPa and a Young's modulus of 33.6 kPa, corresponding to increases of 96.6% and 354%, respectively. In addition, the glass transition temperature and maximum decomposition temperature increased by 13 °C and 12 °C, respectively. The enhanced properties were mainly attributed to hydrogen bonding interactions and the increased crosslinking density within the hydrogel network. Furthermore, the equilibrium swelling degree decreased from 15.6 to 11.3 after incorporation of OH-BNNS and SA. The prepared composite hydrogels demonstrate potential applications in biomedical materials, adsorption, and flexible functional materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed hydroxylated boron nitride nanosheet-reinforced sodium alginate/polyacrylamide hydrogels with substantially higher tensile strength, stiffness, glass-transition temperature, and decomposition temperature than PAM hydrogels. articles.title_original: Waveguide-integrated 2D-material infrared photodetectors: fundamentals, advances, and insights
articles.title_en: Review Surveys Waveguide-Integrated 2D-Material Infrared Photodetectors
articles.excerpt_original: Photodetectors that integrate two-dimensional (2D) materials with optical waveguides are considered an ideal approach to enhance infrared detection capability and on-chip integration capability and have become a focal point of recent research. These devices benefit not only from the intrinsic optoelectronic properties and flexible hetero-integration of 2D materials but also from a range of engineering strategies that enable precise control over their electronic and optical characteristics. In addition, by combining different types of waveguide structures, the optical field distribution can be effectively tailored, further strengthening light-matter interactions and facilitating the realization of compact, high-performance infrared photodetectors with versatile strategies. This review systematically summarizes the latest progress in waveguide-integrated 2D-material infrared photodetectors, organized primarily by the type of waveguide material and further categorized according to the 2D materials employed. It discusses the advantages of various waveguide structures and 2D materials, the working mechanisms, performance parameters, common device architectures, and many key approaches to improving photodetector performance (e.g., waveguide structure optimization, electrode material and spacing design, gate electrostatic doping, substrate engineering, strain modulation, twist angle control of 2D materials, heterojunction band alignment, etc). Furthermore, a comparative analysis with conventional commercial photodetectors is provided, demonstrating that waveguide-integrated 2D-material infrared photodetectors have already achieved comparable performance in many applications, while certain challenges remain. articles.summary_en: The review examines device architectures, mechanisms, materials, and engineering strategies for integrating two-dimensional materials with optical waveguides to improve infrared detection and on-chip integration. articles.title_original: BN-Doped Graphene on Cu(111): Reproducible Growth and Modified π-Band Dispersion
articles.title_en: Reproducible CVD Produces BN-Doped Graphene with Modified Band Dispersion
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Extensive research has been devoted to modifying graphene’s band structure through boron nitride (h-BN) doping. The isostructural and isoelectronic nature of graphene and h-BN makes them ideal candidates for forming hybrid materials that combine the properties of both systems. However, one of the main bottlenecks in achieving this goal has been the lack of a reproducible synthesis route that consistently yields materials with comparable properties. In this work, we present a reproducible chemical vapor deposition (CVD) recipe for the synthesis of boron- and nitrogen-doped graphene (BN-graphene) on Cu(111), which has been successfully reproduced in up to four different setups. The resulting BN-graphene exhibits low BN segregation, with BN domains homogeneously incorporated within the graphene lattice. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) reveals that BN doping modifies the band structure of pristine graphene, leading to a flattening of the π band (valence band). This modified π-band dispersion is consistent with a possible bandgap opening, although the present data do not allow an unambiguous determination of the bandgap.

articles.title_original: Integrated optical isolators enabled by 2D semiconductors via spin-momentum locking
articles.title_en: 2D Semiconductors Enable Integrated Optical Isolators
articles.excerpt_original: Integrated optical isolators based on spin-momentum locking hold great potential for protecting photonic integrated circuits from unwanted reflections. Currently, the most common implementations are magneto-optical isolators that require an externally applied magnetic field. Nevertheless, a wide range of nonreciprocal effects remains to be exploited in alternative material platforms. Although the majority of these effects induce changes to the propagation of light as a function of its polarization, they can be directly connected to the propagation direction through spin-momentum locking. We employ a computational approach to investigate various designs of integrated isolators based on nonreciprocal 2D semiconductors, studying the influence of their geometry and optical properties on the device performance. Additionally, we propose a novel concept for an all-optical isolator based on spin-valley polarization and optically tunable magnetism in transition metal dichalcogenide monolayers. Our results establish 2D semiconductors as an advanced platform for integrated nonreciprocal devices, enabling functionalities that are difficult to achieve with conventional magneto-optical materials like all-optical operation.
articles.summary_en: Computational research explores integrated optical isolators based on spin-momentum locking in nonreciprocal two-dimensional semiconductors. articles.title_original: Synthesis, properties and applications nanoporous carbons with graphene sheets
articles.title_en: Review examines graphene-enhanced nanoporous carbon structures
articles.excerpt_original: Incorporation of graphene layers into amorphous porous carbon affords hybrid carbonaceous nanostructures with a large specific surface area and high porosity originating from nanoporous carbons and enhanced electrical conductivity, and mechanical strength originating from graphene. These hybrid carbon structures are useful for many important applications, including environmental protection (particularly in air and water purification), catalysis, sensors, energy storage, electronics and batteries, tissue engineering, and many others. Since the methods used to produce these materials strongly influence the final pore architecture, as well as their chemical and mechanical properties and consequently, their applications, it is essential to identify correlations between the properties and functionality of such materials. This review provides a detailed assessment of various methods for producing porous carbon structures with graphene layers, with particular emphasis on graphene oxide as a main component. It presents synthesis methods in relation to the resulting morphologies, adsorption properties, mechanical characteristics, and typical applications. Special attention is given to the syntheses that allow for different contents of graphene oxide and its impact on the properties required for specific applications. The main objective of this review is to present various strategies for creating graphene-based nanoporous materials, with particular emphasis on those in which graphene oxide significantly affects the properties of the final material. The review also highlights the relationship between the carbon precursor materials, the synthesis procedures, and the resulting properties, with special focus on adsorption characteristics that determine their potential applications. articles.summary_en: The review assesses synthesis methods for nanoporous carbons incorporating graphene or graphene oxide, linking pore architecture and composition to adsorption, conductivity, and mechanical performance. It highlights potential applications in air and water purification, catalysis, sensors, energy storage, electronics, and tissue engineering.

articles.title_original: Strain-Induced Axial Fields in Graphene as a Condensed-Matter Analogue of Torsion Coupling
articles.title_en: Strain-Induced Axial Fields in Graphene Modelled as Torsion Coupling
articles.excerpt_original: This paper examines how strain in graphene generates an axial gauge field for Dirac carriers that mimics, in form, a torsion coupling, and what energy scales the analogue reaches. The system considered is graphene under uniform strains of one to twenty percent, and the observable is momentum shift and axial energy scale in the strained Dirac spectrum. Evaluating the ordinary behaviour of the system and the spin-torsion contribution under explicit assumptions about polarisation and uniformity, and inverting the comparison at the stated laboratory precision, gives a quantitative bound rather than a qualitative assertion of smallness. The computed record is: rows contains 4 evaluated points; point 1 strain = 0.01; point 1 k_shift_per_m = 1.220e+08; point 1 energy_eV = 0.08027; point 1 pseudo_B_T = None; point 2 strain = 0.05; point 2 k_shift_per_m = 6.098e+08; point 2 energy_eV = 0.4013; point 2 pseudo_B_T = None; point 3 strain = 0.1; point 3 k_shift_per_m = 1.220e+09; point 3 energy_eV = 0.8027; point 3 pseudo_B_T = None; vF_m_s = 1.000e+06; lattice_m = 2.460e-10; energy_at_10pct_eV = 0.8027. The torsion-related contribution is far below the level that would alter the ordinary behaviour of the system at current precision, and the value that would have produced a visible residual is stated so that future improvements can be assessed against it directly. No new measurement is reported. This study is simulated and computed from stated assumptions, not measured.
articles.summary_en: A computational study models how 1–20% uniform strain in graphene generates axial gauge fields and shifts Dirac-carrier momentum. It finds energy scales up to 0.8027 eV at 10% strain, while torsion-related effects remain far below current experimental precision; no measurements are reported.

articles.title_original: Review of the design and development of MXene-based electrocatalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction
articles.title_en: Review surveys MXene-based electrocatalysts for oxygen reduction
articles.excerpt_original: The oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) is a critical half-reaction in fuel cells, but its slow kinetics demand the use of efficient and durable electrocatalysts. MXenes, a novel class of two-dimensional materials, have emerged as highly promising catalyst supports for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) due to their high electrical conductivity, abundant anchoring sites, adjustable surface properties, and excellent durability. This review offers an overview of recent advancements in the design and development of MXene-based electrocatalysts for the ORR. We first introduce common synthesis methods, structural characteristics, and electronic properties of MXenes. Then, we summarize research progress on noble metal catalysts (particularly Pt) using MXenes as supports, as well as non-noble metal catalysts composed of MXenes combined with metal oxides, M-N-C structures, or carbon nanotubes. Moreover, we specifically discuss the theoretical studies of MXene-based single-atom catalysts, which allow efficient activity screening and reaction mechanism elucidation. The application of machine learning in the study of MXene-based ORR electrocatalysts is further reviewed, focusing on how data-driven methods accelerate catalyst discovery and reveal hidden structure-property relationships. Finally, we highlight the major challenges and future research directions, particularly the need to successfully integrate experimental and theoretical studies with machine learning predictions to efficiently explore a broader space of MXene-based electrocatalysts.
articles.summary_en: An academic review examines MXene-supported electrocatalysts for oxygen reduction in fuel cells, covering noble-metal, non-noble-metal and single-atom catalyst designs. It also assesses machine-learning approaches for catalyst discovery and identifies the need to integrate experimental, theoretical and data-driven research.

articles.title_original: Interfacial Solvent Engineering Enables Hydrothermally Stable MXene Heterostructures for Printed Wearable Electronics
articles.title_en: Solvent Engineering Stabilizes MXene for Printed Wearable Devices
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Water-induced degradation of MXene during hydrothermal synthesis severely limits the construction of MXene-based heterostructures for further applications. Herein, an interfacial solvent-engineering strategy was developed to stabilize MXene under harsh hydrothermal conditions. Solvents with a stronger affinity for reactive Ti sites than water can preferentially adsorb at these sites. This competitive adsorption limits direct water–Ti contact and thereby suppresses subsequent MXene oxidation. DFT calculations were used to screen candidate solvents and support the proposed competitive adsorption mechanism, while the experimental results broadly followed the predicted trend. Deoxygenation experiments further supported the dominant role of water in MXene degradation. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that preferential interfacial enrichment of DMF persists at 453 K despite enhanced thermal motion. In a 50 vol % DMF/H2O system, the MXene framework remained well preserved even under prolonged or higher-temperature hydrothermal treatment. This regulated solvent environment enabled the in situ growth of 1T-MoS2 on the preserved MXene framework. The conductive MXene framework and abundant active sites of 1T-MoS2 led to enhanced electrochemical performance. The resulting composite was further processed into printed microsupercapacitors and pressure sensors, which were integrated into a self-powered pressure-sensing system. This work establishes interfacial solvent engineering as an effective route to hydrothermally stable MXene heterostructures for printed wearable electronics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used interfacial solvent engineering to suppress water-induced MXene degradation during hydrothermal processing, enabling in situ growth of 1T-MoS2 heterostructures. The resulting materials were demonstrated in printed microsupercapacitors, pressure sensors, and a self-powered pressure-sensing system.

articles.title_original: Raman Thermometry for Thermal Transport: Principles, Progress and Prospects Across Low‐Dimensional Materials and Devices
articles.title_en: Review Advances in Raman Thermometry for Thermal Transport
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Raman thermometry is widely used to determine thermal‐transport properties from atomically thin membranes to active device regions. Raman‐active phonon modes change predictably with temperature, enabling a focused laser to act as both heater and thermometer. Measurements of the power‐, position‐ or frequency‐dependent Raman response, interpreted with an appropriate heat‐transfer model, can provide in‐plane thermal conductivity and, in selected geometries, interfacial thermal conductance without electrical contacts. Since the first optothermal measurement of suspended monolayer graphene in 2008, the method has been applied to graphene and related carbon materials, transition‐metal dichalcogenides, hexagonal boron nitride, semiconductor nanowires, wide‐bandgap devices and thermoelectric films. Two‐laser, frequency‐domain, transient, Stokes/anti‐Stokes and scanning implementations have extended the technique to supported and device‐integrated specimens. This review examines the physical basis, experimental configurations, heat‐transfer models, results for representative materials and main sources of uncertainty. Particular attention is given to absorptance, beam size, substrate heat leakage, thermomechanical stress and nonequilibrium phonon populations. We conclude with practical guidance on method selection, model validity and uncertainty reporting.
articles.summary_en: The review examines Raman thermometry for measuring thermal conductivity and interfacial thermal conductance in graphene and other low-dimensional materials without electrical contacts. It compares measurement configurations, heat-transfer models, and key uncertainty sources, providing guidance for evaluating thermal transport in supported and device-integrated systems.

articles.title_original: Sulfonate‐Functionalized Boron Nitride Interfacial Layers for Long‐Life Zinc Metal Anodes
articles.title_en: Sulfonate-Functionalized Boron Nitride Enables Long-Life Zinc Anodes
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT The interfacial instability of metallic Zn associated with nonuniform Zn 2 + transport, dendrite growth, hydrogen evolution, and corrosion, limits the durability of aqueous zinc‐ion batteries. In this study, a sulfonate‐bearing artificial interphase was constructed by mixing boron nitride nanosheets (BNNSs) with sodium dodecylbenzene sulfonate (SDBS), followed by scalable spray coating of the suspension onto Zn. The insulating BNNS framework afforded mechanical protection. The negatively charged sulfonate groups improved nanosheet dispersion and Zn 2+ affinity, and regulated interfacial Zn 2+ transport. An SDBS–BNNS@Zn electrode exhibited a lower Zn nucleation overpotential (24.67 mV) and interfacial activation energy (8.31 kJ mol −1 ) compared to BNNS@Zn (25.99 mV and 15.52 kJ mol −1 , respectively). Consequently, symmetric Zn cells exhibited stable plating/stripping for 1100 h at both 0.5 mA cm −2 /0.5 mAh cm −2 and 1 mA cm −2 /1 mAh cm −2 . Ex situ scanning electron microscopy after 1000 h revealed compact, plate‐like Zn deposits, and electrochemical measurements confirmed that hydrogen evolution and corrosion were suppressed. Zn||vanadium oxide full cells exhibited improved capacity, better interfacial kinetics, cycling stability, and an enhanced rate capability. This study presents a simple strategy for conversion of inert BNNSs to ion‐regulating interphases for durable Zn metal anodes.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a spray-coated sulfonate–boron nitride nanosheet interphase that regulates Zn2+ transport while suppressing dendrites, hydrogen evolution, and corrosion. Zinc symmetric cells operated stably for up to 1,100 hours, and zinc–vanadium oxide full cells showed improved cycling and rate performance.

articles.title_original: Reducing TLS Losses in Superconducting Circuits Using Solid Neon
articles.title_en: Solid Neon Treatment Reduces Losses in Superconducting Circuits
articles.excerpt_original: Two level systems (TLSs) are a major source of loss in superconducting devices, limiting the performance of qubits, detectors, and resonators. These defects arise from a range of sources, including surface oxides, crystal defects, as well as fabrication residues which are often difficult to remove. Using NbTiN coplanar waveguide resonators, we show that depositing and subsequently removing a solid neon film can significantly improve device performance. Analysis of the temperature and power dependence indicates that this enhancement arises from reduced TLS dissipation, which we attribute to the redistribution and removal of surface contaminants during neon deposition and evaporation. Atomic force microscopy images of contaminated hexagonal boron nitride flakes before and after neon exposure show that neon treatment can redistribute and remove surface residues. These results demonstrate a simple, non-destructive approach for mitigating TLS losses in superconducting devices and other sensitive materials that cannot withstand aggressive cleaning processes.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report that depositing and removing a solid neon film reduces two-level-system dissipation in NbTiN superconducting resonators. The non-destructive treatment redistributes and removes surface contaminants, potentially benefiting qubits, detectors, and other sensitive devices.

articles.title_original: Band offsets and stability of WSe 2 /RuCl 3 van der Waals charge-transfer contacts
articles.title_en: WSe₂/RuCl₃ contacts show strong charge-transfer band shifts
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The layered Mott insulator α-RuCl 3 induces degenerate hole-doping in two-dimensional semiconductors due to its large electron affinity, making it a promising charge-transfer material for establishing ohmic contacts in electronic devices. In order to assess the applicability and guide the design of devices incorporating RuCl 3 it is critical to determine the electronic structure and robustness of the band offsets that underpin the transport properties of semiconductors in contact with RuCl 3 . Here, we apply micro-focused angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy to determine the electronic structure of single-layer WSe 2 contacted to RuCl 3 on hexagonal boron nitride substrates. We find that formation of a functioning WSe 2 /RuCl 3 contact leads to a valence band shift of (0.68 ± 0.05) eV towards the Fermi energy in WSe 2 . The charge transfer effect is challenging to observe as it depends sensitively on fabrication conditions such as solvent exposure, quality of interface encapsulation and heating of RuCl 3 , imposing strict requirements on device design to attain high-quality contacts.
articles.summary_en: Micro-focused photoemission measurements find a 0.68 ± 0.05 eV valence-band shift in monolayer WSe₂ contacted with RuCl₃, supporting its potential as a charge-transfer material for ohmic contacts. Contact performance is highly sensitive to solvent exposure, interface encapsulation and RuCl₃ heating, imposing stringent fabrication requirements.

articles.title_original: Dielectric engineering of electron mobility in asymmetric Coulomb-coupled GaN quantum wells with hybrid square-triangular confinement
articles.title_en: Dielectric engineering improves mobility in asymmetric GaN quantum wells
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract This work investigates electron mobility in a non-tunneling, Coulomb-coupled GaN bilayer Q2DEG system with asymmetric confinement comprising an infinite-barrier square quantum well and an idealized semi-infinite Fang–Howard triangular-confinement channel. The model combines the distinct wave functions and form factors of the two wells with a three-region dielectric environment, finite-temperature bilayer RPA screening, and the linearized Boltzmann equation. Interface-roughness, charged-dislocation, dislocation-strain-field, and acoustic-phonon scattering are treated with static screening, whereas intrinsic longitudinal-optical-phonon and remote-optical-phonon scattering are treated inelastically with dynamic screening and the Rode iteration. The results show that at 1 K, the mobility is mainly limited by DCS and IRS, whereas LOP and ROP make negligible contributions. At 300 K, acS and LOP become important limiting mechanisms; LOP dominates at high density, whereas HfO₂ provides an additional clear ROP contribution at low density. For the same Sapphire outer regions, h-BN generally gives the highest total mobility, followed by Al₂O₃ and HfO₂, while replacing Sapphire with SiC produces only a relatively small difference. The effective electrostatic interlayer separation has a weak influence, whereas the SQW width strongly modifies IRS: at 1 K, the total mobility reaches a maximum near L = 90 Å; at 300 K, the mobility increases with L over the investigated range and is mainly limited by acS and LOP. An asymmetric density distribution between the two layers shifts or removes the IRS minimum and can increase the total mobility when the SQW layer carries the higher density. articles.summary_en: A modeling study examines electron mobility in asymmetric, Coulomb-coupled GaN bilayer quantum wells under different dielectric environments and confinement conditions. The results identify h-BN as producing the highest mobility among tested dielectrics and show that well width and layer-density asymmetry can substantially influence interface-roughness scattering and overall performance.

articles.title_original: Low-thermal-budget solution-processed montmorillonite dielectric for low-voltage 2D electronics
articles.title_en: Room-temperature montmorillonite dielectric enables low-voltage 2D electronics
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Low-voltage and high-performance electronic devices based on two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors demand high-quality dielectrics with efficient capacitive gating. However, it currently relies on specially engineered atomic layer deposition (ALD) of ultrathin high- k HfO 2 and ZrO 2 , or high-temperature vapor-phase growth of 2D dielectrics with post-growth transfer process. Here, we report a facile solution-processed 2D dielectric with an ultra-low thermal budget (i.e., at room temperature), while delivering competitive device metrics (e.g., low operating voltage and small hysteresis). This is enabled by an organic-free colloidal ink of montmorillonite (MTM) in environmentally friendly water solvent, eliminating the need for organic ligands or surfactants and thus the post-deposition high-temperature thermal annealing. Specifically, all-solution-processed MoS 2 field-effect transistors with MTM dielectric exhibit a low operating voltage of 1 V and small hysteresis (down to 1 mV). The solution process is generally compatible with diverse n-type and p-type 2D semiconductors such as MoS 2 , MoSe 2 and WSe 2 . Moreover, the robust and reproducible MTM dielectric enables scalable device integration into logic circuits, including inverters, AND, NOR, and NAND gates, as well as static random-access memory (SRAM). The scalable room-temperature solution-processed 2D dielectric offers a route to all-solution-processed and low-voltage 2D electronics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed an organic-free, water-based montmorillonite dielectric processed at room temperature, avoiding high-temperature annealing. MoS₂ transistors operated at 1 V with low hysteresis, and the approach supported solution-processed logic circuits and SRAM using multiple 2D semiconductors.

articles.title_original: Low-power 2D CFETs using single-crystal high-κ dielectrics
articles.title_en: Single-Crystal Dielectrics Enable Ultra-Low-Power 2D CFETs
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Aggressive scaling in silicon electronics—although essential for improving power, performance, area and cost—faces increasing challenges in further reducing power consumption due to electrostatic and leakage constraints 1,2 . Achieving efficient operation at low supply voltages therefore requires new materials and gate-stack engineering strategies. Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors offer intrinsic advantages because their atomic thickness affords excellent gate control, and their sizable bandgaps suppress off-state current. However, a major obstacle is the imperfect interface between 2D channels and gate dielectrics, which degrades subthreshold swing, hysteresis and bias-temperature instability 3 . Here we demonstrate that a wafer-scale, transferable, single-crystal anatase titanium dioxide dielectric can be van der Waals integrated with 2D transition metal dichalcogenides. The obtained pristine 2D-dielectric interface enables subthreshold swing close to the thermal limit, record-low hysteresis and well-matched transfer characteristics for both n- and p-type enhancement-mode field-effect transistors. Building on this, we demonstrate complementary field-effect transistors, whose inverters achieve high voltage gain and large noise margins with subpicowatt static power consumption. These results highlight the promise of 2D semiconductors for ultra-low-power operation.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated wafer-scale transferable single-crystal anatase titanium dioxide dielectrics integrated with 2D transition metal dichalcogenides. The resulting complementary transistors achieved near-thermal-limit subthreshold swing, low hysteresis and subpicowatt inverter power consumption, addressing key interface and leakage challenges in advanced low-power electronics.

articles.title_original: Multiscale ensemble Monte Carlo of transport and gas sensing in monolayer MoS 2
articles.title_en: Multiscale Monte Carlo Model Advances MoS₂ Transport and Gas-Sensing Analysis
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Two-dimensional semiconductors, such as monolayer MoS 2 , combine a technologically useful band gap with a thickness of three atomic planes. The entire carrier density then lies within a few Å of the surface, which makes them useful as field-effect-transistor channels and as chemically sensitive devices. Device design for MoS 2 needs a transport model whose scattering rates are computed rather than calibrated, whose predictions are tested against experiment, and that spans the scales from electron-phonon coupling to terminal current and sensor response. We present a self-consistent ensemble Monte Carlo (EMC) framework for monolayer MoS 2 built on the ViennaEMC solver, which couples a Boltzmann transport model to Poisson's equation with degenerate free-carrier statistics. The transport model carries wavevector-dependent acoustic, polar-optical, homopolar and intervalley phonon scattering within and between the K valleys and the spin-orbit-split Q valleys, together with remote substrate phonons, screened charged impurities and surface roughness. Every intrinsic input of the transport model is computed from first principles for this work, namely the band structure of the K and Q valleys, the phonon energies, sound velocities and dielectric response, and the electron-phonon couplings from density-functional perturbation theory (DFPT) matrix elements at 34 explicit phonon wavevectors and from Wannier interpolation with the two-dimensional long-range treatment. The model therefore contains no fitted transport parameter and no coupling taken from another calculation, and its scattering rates are checked against an independent solution of the linearised Boltzmann equation with the same couplings. articles.summary_en: Researchers present a first-principles, self-consistent ensemble Monte Carlo framework for modeling carrier transport and gas-sensing response in monolayer MoS₂. The model incorporates multiple phonon, impurity, substrate, and surface-scattering mechanisms without fitted transport parameters, supporting semiconductor device and sensor design.

articles.title_original: Band geometry, Anderson's theorem, and vortex nucleation in unconventional 2D superconductors
articles.title_en: Band Geometry Alters Disorder Effects in 2D Superconductors
articles.excerpt_original: Motivated by the recent discovery of chiral superconductors in 2d materials, we study the effects of disorder on superconductivity in materials with non-trivial band geometry. First, we show how Anderson's theorem and the conventional Abrikosov-Gorkov description of disorder-induced pair breaking are modified by the structure of the normal-state Bloch functions. We apply these results to twisted MoTe2 and show that a BCS pairing mechanism for the observed superconductor is in tension with the measured normal state residual resistivity. Second, we study whether random potential disorder can nucleate superconducting vortices in a chiral time- reversal-breaking superconductor. We show that, for a superconductor stabilized by the usual BCS mechanism, weak disorder does not induce a vortex glass phase, in contrast to superconductivity formed from an anyon fluid.
articles.summary_en: Researchers develop a framework showing how nontrivial Bloch-state geometry modifies Anderson’s theorem and disorder-induced pair breaking. Applying it to twisted MoTe2, they find conventional BCS pairing is difficult to reconcile with measured residual resistivity and that weak disorder does not produce a vortex-glass phase.

articles.title_original: Matrix-aware 2D field-effect biosensing of cardiac troponin I using complementary ion-sensitive transduction
articles.title_en: Dual 2D sensor platform improves cardiac troponin I detection in serum
articles.excerpt_original: Cardiovascular diseases remain a leading cause of mortality worldwide, highlighting the need for rapid, sensitive and reliable detection of cardiac injury at the point of care. Here, we develop a dual-sensor platform that combines an aptamer-functionalized molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) field-effect transistor (2D-FET) with a graphene-based ion-sensitive field-effect transistor (ISFET) for the detection of cardiac troponin I (Trop-I) in complex biological matrices. The atomically thin MoS2 channel enables highly sensitive detection of Trop-I, achieving a limit of detection of 0.001 ng mL-1. However, the high ionic strength of serum substantially attenuates the field-effect response, resulting in approximately 80% degradation of the sensor response. To address this matrix effect, the ISFET is employed as a secondary sensor to characterize the ionic environment of the sample. Machine-learning-assisted integration of the 2D-FET and ISFET responses is investigated as a strategy for compensating serum-induced signal distortion and recovering key electrical figures of merit extracted from the 2D-FET transfer characteristics, including maximum on-state current (Ids_max), subthreshold slope (SS) and transconductance (gm). This dual-sensor architecture combines molecular recognition, high analytical sensitivity and matrix-aware electrical signal correction, providing a potential pathway towards more reliable FET-based biomarker detection in complex biological fluids. The approach may further enable multiplexed detection of cardiac biomarkers through incorporation of target-specific aptamers, offering potential for broader assessment of cardiac stress and myocardial injury risk.
articles.summary_en: Researchers combined an aptamer-functionalized MoS₂ field-effect transistor with a graphene ion-sensitive transistor to detect cardiac troponin I in complex biological matrices. Machine-learning correction addressed serum-induced signal degradation, supporting more reliable biomarker sensing and potential multiplexed cardiac diagnostics.

articles.title_en: Oxidized Graphene Nanoflakes Adsorb Iodinated Methylene Blue for Melanoma Imaging

articles.title_original: Spatially Confined MXene Core‐Sheath Fibers for Switchable Broadband Microwave Absorption and Terahertz/Infrared Protection
articles.title_en: MXene Core–Sheath Fibers Enable Switchable Multispectral Stealth
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Integrating multispectral stealth with environmental robustness, while maintaining material flexibility, continues to pose a challenge in wearable electromagnetic materials. The orderly assembly of nanoscale electromagnetic units into hierarchically structured fibers imparts vitality to such systems. Herein, a dual‐spatially confined wet‐spinning strategy was proposed to fabricate MXene@Co 3 O 4 (M@C) core‐sheath fibers, selecting aramid nanofiber as the fiber substrate. The synergistic alignment and densification of MXene nanosheets create continuous conductive networks and a built‐in electric field in the core layer, facilitating efficient charge migration and interfacial accumulation for enhanced dielectric loss. Simultaneously, the sheath layer serves as a physical barrier to inhibit MXene oxidation while precisely modulating impedance matching. The resulting M@C fibers demonstrate exceptional mechanical strength and reliability under harsh conditions. The independent regulation across layers enables M@C fibers to achieve a remarkable minimum reflection loss of −55.32 dB and an ultra‐wide effective absorption bandwidth of 6.07 GHz at 2.60 mm. More importantly, the fibers enable orientation‐driven switchable responses originating from anisotropic charge transport and polarization behavior, while the woven fabric realizes multispectral absorption spanning X, Ku, K, and Ka bands, and provides terahertz/infrared protection. This work successfully integrates structural design with independent component optimization, providing a versatile platform for next‐generation wearable electromagnetic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed MXene@Co₃O₄ core–sheath fibers on an aramid nanofiber substrate for broadband microwave absorption and terahertz/infrared protection. The fibers achieved a minimum reflection loss of −55.32 dB and a 6.07 GHz effective absorption bandwidth, with orientation-dependent responses and durability under harsh conditions.

articles.title_original: Arbitrarily cuttable and ultrathin MXene structural colors for customizable and wearable multispectral information management
articles.title_en: Ultrathin MXene structural colors enable cuttable multispectral camouflage
articles.excerpt_original: Structural colors based on natural and artificial microstructures show promising light manipulation. As atomically thick building blocks, Ti 3 C 2 T x sheets have been successfully assembled into the ultrathin, flexible, arbitrarily cuttable, large-size structural colors by the simple and low-cost spray methods based on the lossy thin-film interference. By ordered stacking atomically thick Ti 3 C 2 T x layer by layer at well-organized low–surface tension semidry assemble state, rich colors from yellow to gray with the thickness from ∼22 to ∼154 nanometers of uniform Ti 3 C 2 T x colors are obtained, having the thinnest framework among solution-processed flexible structural colors with similar optical performance. Low-infrared emissivity from room to 300°C temperature and region-selective patterns make highly information-fused and complex visible-infrared (VIS-IR) Ti 3 C 2 T x colors camouflage. Without conventional dielectric layer between Ti 3 C 2 T x and substrate, automated spraying system can produce meter-scale films that can be cut and sewn into VIS-IR concealment “camouflage cloaks” easily, promising ultrathin multifunctional information systems and beyond.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed meter-scale, spray-assembled Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene films with tunable visible colors, low infrared emissivity, and flexible, cuttable form factors. The films can be sewn into wearable VIS–IR camouflage, suggesting applications in defense and multifunctional information systems.

articles.title_original: Ultrasensitive Optoelectronic Synapse in Mixed‐Dimensional CuInSe 2 Nanowires/MoS 2 Heterostructures
articles.title_en: CuInSe₂/MoS₂ Heterostructure Enables High-Performance Optoelectronic Synapse
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Mixed‐dimensional semiconductor heterostructures offer a compelling platform for combining photodetection with optoelectronic synaptic functionalities through controlled photocarrier dynamics. Here, we report catalyst‐free chemical vapor deposition growth of p‐type one‐dimensional CuInSe 2 (CIS) nanowires and their integration with n‐type two‐dimensional MoS 2 to construct mixed‐dimensional p‐n heterojunctions. Individual CIS nanowires exhibit pronounced defect‐assisted photoconductive gain and optoelectronic synaptic behaviors, yet suffer from high dark current that limits weak‐light detection. By establishing a CIS/MoS 2 heterostructure, the band alignment promotes the transition from majority hole conduction in CIS to electron‐dominated conduction in the heterostructure, resulting in strong suppression of dark current and markedly enhanced optoelectronic performance, including a responsivity up to 2286 A·W −1 , an ultrahigh detectivity of 9.29 × 10 12 Jones, and external quantum efficiency exceeding 4.45 × 10 5 %, while retaining the short‐term memory functionalities. Leveraging this short‐term memory response as a temporal preprocessing layer, the synaptic heterostructure device enables device‐calibrated simulations for proof‐of‐concept visual‐processing tasks in handwritten‐digit classification, motion‐direction recognition, and next‐position prediction. This work establishes carrier‐dynamics engineering in 1D/2D p‐n heterostructures as an effective strategy to connect photodetection with neuromorphic optoelectronics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed catalyst-free CuInSe₂ nanowires integrated with MoS₂ to form mixed-dimensional p–n heterojunctions. The device suppresses dark current while achieving high responsivity and detectivity, supporting proof-of-concept neuromorphic visual-processing tasks.

articles.title_original: Layer-Number-Controlled Symmetry Breaking and Surface-State Transport in Rhombohedral Graphene Multilayers
articles.title_en: Layer Number Tunes Symmetry Breaking in Rhombohedral Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Rhombohedral multilayer graphene hosts layer-polarized flat bands, providing an intriguing platform for correlated and topological states; however, how layer number governs symmetry breaking and surface screening remains elusive. Here, we prepare rhombohedral graphene multilayers and systematically conduct electrical transport measurements. We uncover an unconventional layer dependence of phase transitions: the critical displacement field Dc for the layer-antiferromagnetic-to-semimetal transitions remains nearly constant across tetralayer to hexalayer graphene, whereas Dc for the semimetal-to-layer-polarized-insulator transition increases with layer number, defying unscreened Coulomb interaction models. In hexalayer graphene, surface-state-dominated transport emerges with Landau levels and resistive peaks predominantly controlled by adjacent gates, revealing strong interlayer screening. High magnetic fields further reveal valley-layer-locked Landau levels and dissipative states associated with interlayer backscattering, highlighting the presence of decoupled surface states. Our findings establish the layer number as a key tuning knob for engineering correlated and topological phases in rhombohedral graphene multilayers.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that graphene layer number controls phase transitions, screening, and surface-state transport in rhombohedral multilayers. The findings identify layer thickness as a tuning parameter for correlated and topological semiconductor devices.

articles.title_original: MXene-PS-Based Soft Actuator with Deformation Reversal Capability through Time-Sequence Difference of Asymmetric Water Absorption Kinetics
articles.title_en: MXene-PS Bilayer Actuator Enables Reversible Deformation and Self-Sustained Motion
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Many soft actuators have been developed to achieve bending deformation under external stimuli through asymmetric structures or nonuniform material distributions. However, most existing actuators can only produce bending in a single direction, and developing soft actuators with deformation reversal capability remains a challenge. To address this issue, this study proposes an MXene-PS/MXene bilayer soft actuator, which is fabricated by sequential vacuum-assisted filtration, resulting in a loose MXene-PS top layer and a dense MXene bottom layer. The MXene-PS layer features a high water absorption/desorption rate but low capacity, while the MXene layer exhibits a low rate but high capacity. This complementary kinetic-capacity coupling mechanism, termed the time-sequence difference of asymmetric water absorption kinetics, enables the actuator to achieve reversible deformation reversal under NIR light and humidity stimuli. Furthermore, simply by changing the placement orientation of the actuator, two distinct self-sustained oscillation behaviors can be obtained in a humidity gradient environment, namely, periodic motion toward or away from the water surface. Leveraging this deformation reversal capability, we demonstrate two proof-of-concept applications: a biomimetic flower and a self-sustained motion sailboat. This work introduces a deformation mode and actuation principle for MXene-based soft actuators and further broadens their application prospects in biomimetic devices and soft robotics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a bilayer MXene-PS/MXene soft actuator that reverses deformation under near-infrared light and humidity by exploiting different water-absorption kinetics. Demonstrations included a biomimetic flower and a self-propelled sailboat, suggesting potential for soft robotics and biomimetic systems.
