articles.title_original: Toward information transfer by graphene in the terahertz regime
articles.title_en: Graphene Demonstrates Terahertz Information Transfer Over Hundreds of Micrometers
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Graphene supports highly confined, tunable surface-plasmon waves in the terahertz regime, making it a promising candidate for information transfer in next-generation integrated circuitry. We solved the classical time-domain Maxwell equations to determine the response of a graphene half-plane excited by a carrier plane wave amplitude-modulated by a narrow-width pulse, employing a recently formulated finite-element time-domain method with a perfectly matched layer. Detectability loss, Pearson correlation coefficient, and concordance coefficient were computed to assess signal fidelity between transmission and reception points. Simulations across varied pulse widths and carrier frequencies consistently yield Pearson correlations of approximately 91% and concordance coefficients of approximately 55%, with information-transfer distances reaching hundreds of micrometers. Lower carrier frequencies extend the absolute transfer distance. These findings establish graphene as a viable information-carrying medium in the terahertz gap.
articles.summary_en: IOP Publishing research uses time-domain Maxwell simulations to assess graphene surface-plasmon information transfer in the terahertz regime. The modeled system achieved approximately 91% Pearson correlation and transfer distances of hundreds of micrometers, indicating potential for integrated-circuit communications.

articles.title_original: Hierarchical 3D Bilayer Magnetic Foam/MXene Film Composites for High‐Performance Absorption‐Driven Electromagnetic Interference Shielding
articles.title_en: Bilayer graphene–MXene foam reaches 82.65 dB EMI shielding
articles.excerpt_original: Polymer composites exhibiting absorption‐dominated electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding with minimal reflection are highly attractive for advanced electronic systems due to their ability to minimize secondary electromagnetic radiation pollution. However, achieving high EMI shielding that is primarily governed by microwave absorption‐dominated attenuation remains a significant technical hurdle. In this work, we developed a bilayer foam/film structure consisting of porous magnetic graphene nanoplatelet (GnP)@zinc ferrite (ZnFe 2 O 4 )/polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) foam and conductive MXene/PDMS film. This is assembled through a combined method using a simple and cost‐effective sugar‐template approach, along with a layer‐on‐layer casting strategy. The bilayer configuration enables the porous GnP@ZnFe 2 O 4 /PDMS foam to function as an effective microwave absorption layer, while the MXene/PDMS film acts as a robust reflection layer. This integrated bilayer structural synergy promotes a multiple scattering and successive absorption–reflection–reabsorption process, resulting in an outstanding absorption coefficient of 0.79 and a remarkable EMI shielding effectiveness of 82.65 dB. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of combining magnetic foams with conductive films to achieve highly efficient EMI shielding materials with prominent direction‐dependent absorption features.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a porous magnetic graphene nanoplatelet/zinc ferrite–PDMS foam paired with a conductive MXene–PDMS film for absorption-driven electromagnetic interference shielding. The bilayer achieved an absorption coefficient of 0.79 and shielding effectiveness of 82.65 dB, indicating potential for advanced electronics and defense-related electromagnetic protection.

articles.title_original: Interface-Driven Remote-Surface States in Rhombohedral Graphene
articles.title_en: Rhombohedral Graphene Shows Remote-Surface Electronic States
articles.excerpt_original: Rhombohedral multilayer graphene hosts low-energy states on its two outer surfaces. We identify a layer-by-layer mechanism through which a low-energy state generated at one surface acquires weight on successive layers up to the opposite surface. For an outer-layer vacancy, the wavefunction spreads over a larger area on successive layers, shifting normalized weight toward the remote surface as the system size increases. The same relation governs the extension of sublattice-polarized zero modes bound to circular voids and straight zigzag terminations. At periodic moire interfaces, it acts separately on each momentum harmonic, making the layer polarization of the low-energy bands depend on Bloch momentum and modulation period. This provides an intrinsic single-particle explanation for the remote-surface modulations observed in recent multilayer graphene experiments.
articles.summary_en: Researchers identify a layer-by-layer mechanism that transfers low-energy wavefunction weight between the outer surfaces of rhombohedral multilayer graphene. The findings explain momentum- and period-dependent layer polarization at moiré interfaces and could inform future graphene-based electronic devices.

articles.title_original: An organic semiconductor-based photocatalyst sheet for overall solar-driven water splitting
articles.title_en: Organic semiconductor sheet enables solar-driven water splitting
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using sunlight offers a route to renewable fuel, but translating this reaction into systems suitable for industrial implementation remains difficult. Photocatalyst sheets can overcome key limitations of common direct water-splitting approaches (photoelectrochemical devices and photocatalyst dispersions), but existing photocatalyst sheets rely on inorganic semiconductor nanoparticles and processing techniques that can be difficult to scale. Here we show that solution-processed organic semiconductors can form water-splitting photocatalyst sheets by simply tailoring the charge extraction layer beneath the light-absorbing film. A single organic semiconductor active layer (deposited as a bulk heterojunction blend) drives either hydrogen or oxygen evolution depending on its underlying molecular contact, yielding photocathode and photoanode half-cells with well-matched photocurrents. Combining both reactions on one substrate using a microdomain-patterned molecular underlayer affords a photocatalyst sheet that achieves unassisted water splitting under simulated sunlight for over 2 h and generates hydrogen at a stabilized rate of 1.3 µmol h −1 cm −2 , which corresponds to a solar-to-hydrogen conversion efficiency of 0.1%.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a solution-processed organic semiconductor photocatalyst sheet that separates water into hydrogen and oxygen under simulated sunlight. The device operated for more than two hours, producing hydrogen at 1.3 µmol h⁻¹ cm⁻² with a solar-to-hydrogen efficiency of 0.1%, but industrial scalability remains unproven.

articles.title_original: Enhancing the Photocatalytic Performance of CuBi2O4 Through Graphene Oxide Incorporation
articles.title_en: Graphene Oxide Enhances CuBi2O4 Photocatalytic Dye Removal
articles.excerpt_original: Copper bismuth oxide (CuBi2O4) was produced through a domestic microwave-assisted synthesis using water as an environmentally friendly solvent, whereas graphene oxide (GO) was obtained using a modified Hummers’ method. Structural characterization by XRD confirmed the formation of a pristine tetragonal CuBi2O4 phase, with no shift in diffraction peaks after GO incorporation, although a slight reduction in crystallinity was observed. FESEM analysis revealed the characteristic sheet-like morphology of GO and spherical CuBi2O4 particles. EDS analysis verified the elemental composition of the prepared composites. Incorporating GO into CuBi2O4 narrowed the optical band gap from 2.4 to 2.2 eV and suppressed electron–hole recombination, as evidenced by the lower photoluminescence intensity. Furthermore, BET measurements showed that the specific surface area increased markedly from 3.79 m2/g for pristine CuBi2O4 to 16.49 m2/g for the composite. This enhancement may provide additional adsorption sites for malachite green (MG) molecules, promoting their adsorption onto the composite surface before exposure to visible light. The composite achieved 86.5% MG removal within 150 min, with nearly twice the rate constant of pristine CuBi2O4. Reactive species trapping experiments indicated that photogenerated holes (h+) and superoxide radicals (•O2−) played major roles in the photocatalytic process. Meanwhile, the removal efficiency of pristine CuBi2O4 declined by approximately 40% after four consecutive reuse cycles.
articles.summary_en: A graphene oxide–CuBi2O4 composite narrowed the band gap, increased surface area, and reduced electron–hole recombination. It removed 86.5% of malachite green within 150 minutes, nearly doubling the pristine material’s reaction rate.

articles.title_original: Design and Simulation of CMUT Based on Graphene/Parylene-C Composite Membrane
articles.title_en: Graphene–Parylene-C Membrane Simulated for CMUT Ultrasound Arrays
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract This paper proposes a capacitive micromachined ultrasonic transducer (CMUT) cell with a graphene/Parylene-C composite membrane, which takes full advantage of the excellent mechanical flexibility, low mass density and favorable electrical properties of the composite material to improve the electromechanical coupling efficiency and overall output performance of the ultrasonic transducer. A multi-physics finite-element model is established, and systematic parametric sweeps are carried out to investigate how key structural parameters including cavity radius, cavity height and membrane thickness influence the resonant frequency and dynamic vibration characteristics of the CMUT cell. According to the simulated results, optimal structural parameters are determined for the unit cell. On this basis, a CMUT phased array is designed targeting the operating resonant frequency of the optimized cell, and its acoustic directivity as well as beam-focusing performance are assessed via acoustic field numerical simulations. The simulation demonstrates that the developed composite-membrane CMUT phased array exhibits promising application potential for medical focused ultrasound imaging, and lays a simulation-driven foundation for the subsequent design and practical development of CMUT devices.

articles.title_original: Polarization-insensitive silicon nitride AWG using double-layer waveguides
articles.title_en: Polarization-Insensitive Silicon Nitride AWG Demonstrated
articles.excerpt_original: The arrayed waveguide grating (AWG) is a core dispersive component in on-chip spectroscopic detection systems, but its polarization sensitivity can degrade spectral calibration and reconstruction accuracy. In this Letter, we propose a synchronous phase-matching method for polarization-insensitive AWG design, which is related to the propagation phases at both the center wavelength and the whole range of the working wavelength. Two different cross-sections of double-layer silicon nitride (Si 3 N 4 ) waveguides were designed to achieve polarization-insensitive outputs for a coarse and a fine AWG, respectively. Numerical simulations demonstrate that polarization-dependent wavelength shift (PDWS) below 0.165 nm with polarization-dependent loss (PDL) less than 0.214 dB has been obtained for TE and TM polarizations on a nine-channel AWG under a spectral channel spacing of 2.74 nm. Furthermore, a PDWS below 17.1 pm with a PDL less than 0.169 dB has been obtained for a seven-channel fine AWG with a channel spacing of 0.12 nm.
articles.summary_en: Researchers proposed a synchronous phase-matching design for polarization-insensitive arrayed waveguide gratings using double-layer silicon nitride waveguides. Simulations showed reduced polarization-dependent wavelength shift and loss in both coarse and fine nine- and seven-channel AWGs, supporting on-chip spectroscopic detection.

articles.title_original: Electronic Origin of Contrasting Li and Na Clustering on Graphene
articles.title_en: Study Explains Li and Na Clustering on Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: The electrochemical performance of anode materials is often defined by the ability of metal ions (e.g., Li and Na) to be effectively stored within the host material over a specific range of chemical potentials. This is particularly true for adsorbed Li and Na atoms on carbon surfaces (e.g., graphite or pore surfaces in hard carbon), where the interplay between ionic and metallic bonding often takes place - while metal atoms act as ionic species, in a finite concentration limit, they tend to form metallic bonding when they approach each other. What makes the case special is that, despite similar chemical identities, Li and Na atoms exhibit distinct tendencies for cluster formation; for example, the formation of Li metallic clusters on a graphene surface is only thermodynamically favorable after reaching a finite metal-ion concentration. Motivated by this, herein, we use first-principles calculations on graphene to examine the electronic origin of Li and Na clustering. Specifically, we demonstrate that the separated adsorbed atoms donate electrons to graphene, shifting the Fermi level to higher energies; however, the formation of metal clusters can result in the formation of lower-energy orbitals that are specifically associated with metal-metal bonding, thus lowering the Fermi level (and hence total energies). Importantly, while the process is somewhat similar for Na and Li atoms, the energy levels of the newly formed metallic states govern the difference in metallic cluster formation between Li and Na.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations show that Li and Na atoms donate electrons to graphene, while clustering creates lower-energy metal–metal bonding states. Differences in these electronic states explain why Li clustering becomes favorable only above a threshold concentration and why Li and Na behave differently as graphene-hosted anode species.

articles.title_original: Enhanced Optical Absorption of Graphene Using a Distributed Bragg Reflector Cavity

articles.excerpt_original: In this paper, we demonstrate enhanced absorption of nearly 92% from a monolayer of graphene using a distributed Bragg reflector (DBR) resonator. The DBR consists of alternating layers of Ge and SiO2, with the graphene surrounded by Ge or Si in two different layer configurations that are convenient for implementation in a Schottky Barrier photodetector. This method has the potential to increase the external quantum efficiency of Schottky Barrier photodetectors using graphene/Si or graphene/Ge interfaces, and enable inexpensive infrared photodetection in silicon platforms with high external quantum efficiencies.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated nearly 92% optical absorption in monolayer graphene using a distributed Bragg reflector cavity made from alternating germanium and silicon dioxide layers. The approach could improve external quantum efficiency in graphene/silicon or graphene/germanium Schottky-barrier photodetectors for low-cost infrared sensing.

articles.excerpt_original: This work presents a structured instructional approach for introducing charge transfer at molecule-surface interfaces in upper-level undergraduate or graduate chemistry curricula.Using graphene as a representative two-dimensional material, molecular electronic descriptors are organized into a unified visual diagram that supports student understanding of doping behavior.The diagram integrates concepts from molecular orbital theory, chemical hardness, and band structure within a format designed for classroom adoption.Guided examples illustrate how students can classify molecular adsorbates according to p-type, n-type, or negligible charge-transfer regimes using readily accessible molecular properties.The accompanying Supporting Information provides a lesson plan outlining course placement, prerequisite knowledge, suggested instructional pacing, and assessment strategies.By offering a coherent and transferable 1 visualization tool, this text aims to facilitate interdisciplinary integration of surface chemistry concepts across physical chemistry, materials chemistry, and nanoscience courses.

articles.title_original: Direct patterning single-layer CVD graphene by oxidation scanning probe lithography
articles.title_en: Resist-Free Lithography Patterns 10 nm Graphene Nanoribbons
articles.excerpt_original: Single-layer graphene, with its atomic thickness and exceptional properties, offers great opportunities for high-performance nanoscale devices. While patterning is essential for translating the unique properties of graphene into functional devices, conventional ultraviolet (UV) lithography and electron-beam lithography (EBL) are constrained by limited resolution, resist residues and crystal damage. Here, we report nanoscale patterning of single-layer chemical vapor deposition (CVD) graphene using high-resolution, resist-free oxidation scanning probe lithography (o-SPL). By applying an alternating voltage to an electrically conductive probe, we demonstrate maskless, direct writing of graphene nanostructures on insulating substrates through the electrochemical reaction of graphene with water molecules. The dimensions of the patterned structures can be controlled by the voltage amplitude and probe scanning velocity, enabling single-layer graphene nanoribbons with widths down to ∼10 nm. This work highlights o-SPL as a precise and clean approach for patterning two-dimensional materials and functional devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated direct, maskless patterning of single-layer CVD graphene using oxidation scanning probe lithography, avoiding resist residues and crystal damage associated with conventional methods. The technique produced graphene nanoribbons as narrow as approximately 10 nm, supporting nanoscale device fabrication.

articles.title_original: Enhanced Properties of Copper Matrix Composites Reinforced With In Situ Prepared Cr‐Doped Graphene
articles.title_en: Cr-Doped Graphene Strengthens Copper Matrix Composites
articles.excerpt_original: To suppress graphene agglomeration and improve Cu/graphene interfacial characteristics, this work employs graphene oxide (GO) and Cr sulfate solution. Cr particles are introduced into graphene nanosheets via in situ chemical reduction in a water bath for 3 h. The resulting powder was mixed with copper powder, compacted, and sintered at 950 °C for 90 min. Cr doping may improve graphene dispersion and the interfacial interaction between graphene and copper. Cr‐doped graphene prepared using 0.05 mol/L Cr sulfate and glucose exhibits the most favorable morphology and dispersion under the investigated conditions. X‐ray diffraction (XRD) analysis indicates the presence of a metallic Cr phase, while Raman analysis suggests that the graphene‐based sp 2 carbon framework is retained after Cr modification. Within the investigated addition range from 0 to 1.0 wt.%, the copper matrix composite containing 0.5 wt.% Cr‐doped graphene exhibits favorable comprehensive properties. Cr‐doped graphene is relatively homogeneously dispersed in the copper matrix. The hardness and tensile strength reach 85.6 HV and 245 MPa, respectively, representing increases of 77.6% and 36% compared with pure copper. The electrical conductivity reaches 91.29% IACS. Tensile fracture morphologies of composites present ductile fracture characteristic, and the improved graphene dispersion and metallurgical bonding of Cu/graphene interface is favorable for load transfer.
articles.summary_en: Researchers prepared chromium-doped graphene in situ and incorporated it into sintered copper composites. At 0.5 wt.% addition, the composite reached 85.6 HV hardness, 245 MPa tensile strength, and 91.29% IACS conductivity, attributed to improved graphene dispersion and copper interfacial bonding.

For each MXene: 0 K formation energy, decomposition energy, energy above the convex hull, decomposition products, band gap and layer group, plus the relaxed structure (VASP CONTCAR). Competing phases were retrieved from the Materials Project and recomputed with r2SCAN. Naming convention: <category><n>-<M><M'><X>, e.g. o2-ScYC, i1-YScC. For o-MXenes the first metal occupies the inner layer(s); for i-MXenes the first metal occupies 2/3 of the metal sites.
articles.summary_en: Researchers present a computational dataset of 1,040 bare, delaminated, ordered binary and ternary MXenes. It reports formation and decomposition energies, stability, band gaps, layer groups, and relaxed structures for MXenes containing transition metals with carbon or nitrogen.

articles.title_original: High-Fidelity In Silico Dataset of Ordered Binary and Ternary MXenes with Predictive Synthesis Guidance
articles.title_en: DFT Dataset Identifies Synthesizable MXenes and Processing Conditions
articles.excerpt_original: Despite their promise, the targeted synthesis of novel MXenes remains challenging due to their vast structural and compositional space and the lack of reliable stability descriptors that account for synthesis conditions. To address this gap, we utilized density functional theory (DFT) with the r$^2$SCAN functional to develop a high-fidelity dataset of 1,040 ordered binary and ternary bare delaminated MXenes, including mono-transition metal MXenes, in-plane ordered double-transition metal MXenes, in-plane ordered metal-divacancy MXenes, and out-of-plane ordered double-transition-metal MXenes. For each structure, we calculated formation and decomposition Gibbs energies, decomposition products, layer symmetry groups, and energies above the hull. We find that all MXenes are thermodynamically inaccessible under equilibrium conditions. However, 115 predominantly carbide MXenes become thermodynamically stabilized at elevated temperatures (500--2000 K), and 23 are stabilized under high pressure (10 GPa). Additionally, three MXenes in the Mn--Fe--C chemical space are stabilized within an experimentally feasible range of carbon chemical potentials. These findings reveal stability trends across the MXene space and identify synthesis strategies that can guide experimental efforts. Our dataset provides a robust foundation for developing machine-learned stability descriptors and for guiding experimental efforts toward novel MXene discovery. By identifying synthesizable candidates along with their synthesis conditions, this work bridges a critical gap in data-driven approaches to MXene discovery and lays the foundation for future autonomous experimental workflows.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a high-fidelity dataset of 1,040 ordered binary and ternary MXenes using density functional theory. The study identifies candidates stabilized by elevated temperature, high pressure, or specific carbon chemical potentials, providing guidance for experimental synthesis.

articles.title_original: Evaluating the growth and publication patterns of MXene research: a bibliometric analysis using Bradford’s law of scattering
articles.title_en: Bibliometric Analysis Maps MXene Research Growth and Publication Patterns
articles.summary_en: An academic study evaluates the growth and publication patterns of MXene research using Bradford’s law of scattering. The analysis concerns research-literature distribution rather than a specific commercial application or company.

articles.title_original: Micro-nanocomposite films with enhanced mechanical and barrier properties by non-destructive exfoliation and self-assembly of MXene/polyamide 6
articles.title_en: MXene–Polyamide Films Deliver Stronger Mechanical and Gas-Barrier Performance
articles.excerpt_original: The inferior dispersibility and poor interfacial interaction with the matrix substantially restricted the reinforcing effects of two-dimensional (2D) nanosheets on the composites. Here, large-sized and ultrathin LiHL-Ti 3 C 2 T x (LiHL-MXene) nanoflakes were successfully prepared by an organic solvent-assisted intercalation strategy, which effectively prevented fragmentation of nanoflakes without ultrasonic process under the advantage of low energy consumption. According to thermal stress induction, MXene nanoflakes were uniformly assembled within the polyamide 6 (PA6) matrix to construct a robust brick-and-mortar interface structure, thereby achieving reinforcement across multiple length scales. Benefiting from the homogeneous distribution of nanoflakes and strong filler-matrix interfacial interactions, the tensile strength and toughness of PA6/LiHL-MXene composites reached 67.81 MPa and 130.86 MJ/m 3 . By introducing the finite element representative volume elements (RVEs), stress–strain curves of uniaxial tensile testing were simulated and the coupling mechanisms between microstructure and mechanical behaviors were explored. High orientation and large contact area of LiHL-MXene effectively hindered the diffusion of gases to endow the composites with excellent barrier properties (oxygen permeability coefficient: 0.87 × 10 –17 mol·m/m 2 ·s·Pa; hydrogen permeability coefficient: 0.75 × 10 –16 mol·m/m 2 ·s·Pa). This work provided a feasible approach for developing next-generation high-performance barrier films, demonstrating applications in the fields of storage and transportation of gases.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed ultrathin MXene/polyamide 6 films using non-destructive exfoliation and self-assembly, achieving improved tensile strength, toughness, and exceptionally low oxygen and hydrogen permeability. The results support potential use in gas storage and transport barrier films.

articles.title_original: Introduction to 2D quantum materials
articles.title_en: Introduction to 2D Quantum Materials and Graphene’s Discovery
articles.excerpt_original: The field of two-dimensional (2D) materials, though relatively young, has fundamentally transformed condensed matter physics, nanoscience, and materials engineering over the past two decades. Its origins are rooted in the long-standing theoretical curiosity about the behavior of matter confined to a single atomic plane. For many years, such systems were considered largely hypothetical. A central argument against their existence arose from the Mermin-Wagner theorem [1], which predicts that long-range crystalline order in strictly 2D systems should be destabilized at finite temperatures due to thermal fluctuations. As a result, it was widely believed that free-standing 2D crystals could not exist in a stable form under ambient conditions. Despite these theoretical constraints, the landscape of materials science changed dramatically in 2004, when Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at the University of Manchester successfully isolated graphene, a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice, from bulk graphite. Their approach, known as mechanical exfoliation or the "Scotch tape method," [2] was remarkably simple yet profoundly effective. By repeatedly peeling layers from graphite using adhesive tape, they were able to obtain atomically thin flakes and identify monolayer graphene on a substrate using optical microscopy and spectroscopy techniques. This breakthrough demonstrated that 2D crystals could indeed exist as stable, free-standing entities, largely due to intrinsic rippling and out-of-plane deformations that stabilize the lattice against thermal fluctuations. The discovery of graphene not only challenged existing theoretical assumptions but also unveiled a material with extraordinary physical properties, including exceptionally high carrier mobility,
articles.summary_en: This academic overview examines the foundations of two-dimensional materials and the theoretical challenges surrounding their stability. It highlights the 2004 isolation of graphene by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at the University of Manchester, which demonstrated the viability of stable 2D crystals and established graphene as a foundational material for nanoscience and engineering.

articles.title_original: Unveiling the Phase Transformation Mechanism in BN from Large-Scale Machine Learning Molecular Dynamics
articles.title_en: Machine-learning simulations reveal phase-transformation pathways in boron nitride
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Boron nitride (BN) exhibits rich polymorphism, including cubic, hexagonal, rhombohedral, and wurtzite phases, whose dynamic transformations govern the stability and performance of BN-based materials in modern electronics, quantum photonics, and energy devices. Despite their technological importance, the atomistic mechanisms underlying its phase evolution remain poorly understood. Here, we use large-scale molecular dynamics simulations with a MACE-based machine learning interatomic potential. The potential is trained on high-fidelity density functional theory data and validated against ab initio molecular dynamics simulations to investigate phase transformation pathways in crystalline BN. We identify a layer-by-layer transformation mechanism that is initiated at heterogeneous BN interfaces, where local structural reconstruction propagates into neighboring crystalline regions. We further show that the transformation propensity depends on the interfacial structure and crystallographic orientation. These results provide atomistic insight into BN phase transformations under diverse thermodynamic conditions, while the associated MACE training workflow offers a generalizable framework for studying phase transformation mechanisms in other complex materials.
articles.summary_en: Large-scale molecular dynamics simulations identify a layer-by-layer boron nitride phase-transformation mechanism initiated at heterogeneous interfaces. The findings link transformation propensity to interfacial structure and crystallographic orientation, offering insights relevant to electronic and photonic BN materials.

articles.title_original: Decoupling Metal Deposition from Contact Formation Enables Polarity Transformation in WSe2 Transistors
articles.title_en: Removable Semimetal Layers Enable Polarity Switching in WSe₂ Transistors
articles.excerpt_original: Polarity control in two-dimensional (2D) semiconductor field-effect transistors (FETs) is essential for their integration into complementary logic circuits. However, existing polarity-engineering approaches often fail to preserve high-quality contact interfaces because atomically thin 2D semiconductors are highly sensitive to fabrication processes. Here, we introduce an effective buffer-layer removal process that enables polarity transformation while preserving a high-quality contact interface. A thin semimetal layer (Bi or Sb) is deposited prior to high-work-function metal evaporation and subsequently removed by a wet chemical treatment that preserves a high-quality metal/semiconductor interface. Minimizing the contact angle of the rinsing solution suppresses wrinkle and bubble formations and reduces Fermi-level pinning. The same WSe2 transistors transform from semimetal-dominated n-type transport before treatment to high-work-function-metal-dominated p-type transport afterward. Monolayer devices exhibit a maximum two-terminal hole field-effect mobility of 313 cm2 V-1 s-1 after treatment, while also supporting a maximum electron mobility of 41 cm2 V-1 s-1 before treatment. These results demonstrate n-to-p polarity transformation in WSe2 transistors enabled by a removable semimetal layer, providing a potential doping-free route toward complementary 2D electronics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated reversible n-to-p polarity transformation in WSe₂ transistors by removing a temporary bismuth or antimony buffer layer after high-work-function metal deposition. The process preserved contact quality and achieved hole mobility up to 313 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹, offering a potential doping-free route to complementary 2D electronics.

articles.title_original: Two-dimensional indium selenide (InSe): fundamentals, synthesis strategies, and next- generation optoelectronic device architecture
articles.title_en: Review assesses indium selenide for next-generation optoelectronics
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional (2D) layered semiconductors have garnered significant interest as promising candidates for next-generation optoelectronic applications, owing to their tunable electronic band structures, high surface-to-volume ratios, and pronounced light-matter interactions. Among this growing family of materials, van der Waals indium selenide (InSe) has emerged as a particularly attractive candidate for future high-mobility optoelectronic devices, such as high-performance photodetectors, polarisation-sensitive devices, and chemical sensors. This is primarily due to its thickness-dependent bandgap, high intrinsic carrier mobility, and strong optical absorption. Compared with other extensively investigated 2D materials, InSe combines a comparatively high electron mobility with a layer-tunable band gap and spectral response extending from the visible to near-infrared region, whereas graphene lacks a band gap and MoS 2 shows weak near-infrared absorption. Its practical advantage, however, depends on encapsulation, contact quality, and phase control. This review provides a comprehensive and critical assessment of recent advances in InSe-based photodetectors, with particular emphasis on their crystal structure, electronic properties, synthesis methodologies, and device engineering strategies. Various fabrication techniques, including mechanical exfoliation, liquid-phase exfoliation, chemical vapor deposition, and physical vapor deposition routes (physical vapor transport, pulsed laser deposition, molecular beam epitaxy, and thermal evaporation) are systematically discussed in relation to their impact on material quality and device performance, together with the transfer and device fabrication steps that link the material to the photodetector. Furthermore, the fundamental pho
articles.summary_en: A review examines two-dimensional indium selenide (InSe), highlighting its tunable bandgap, high carrier mobility and visible-to-near-infrared response for photodetectors, polarization-sensitive devices and chemical sensors. It also evaluates synthesis, encapsulation, contacts and phase control as key factors affecting device performance.

articles.title_original: Plasmons of graphene and monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides double-layer
articles.title_en: Graphene–TMD Bilayers Show Tunable Plasmon Modes
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract We investigate the plasmonic properties of a double-layer structure consisting of graphene and monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (ML-TMDs) separated by a space distance d where the carrier densities in different layers are n 1 and n 2 within the usual standard random-phase approximation dielectric function approach. There exists two branches of plasmons for an acoustical mode and an optical mode, respectively. We examine the effect of carrier density, inter-layer spacing, and types of TMDs materials on the plasmon properties. Meanwhile, the two branches of plasmons have nonzero decay rates after entering the Landau damping regions for intra-band and inter-band single-particle excitation continuum. The plasmons in double-layer structure exhibit significant tunability, offering promising applications of 2D materials for plasmonic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers modeled plasmonic behavior in double-layer structures combining graphene with monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides. Carrier density, layer spacing, and TMD type tune acoustic and optical plasmon branches, supporting potential plasmonic-device applications.

articles.title_original: Supermoiré reconstruction and domain-resolved valley topology in helical multilayer graphene
articles.title_en: Helical multilayer graphene reveals tunable valley topology
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Extending moiré graphene beyond twisted bilayers, helical trilayer graphene has emerged as a supermoiré platform hosting topological bands and correlated electronic states. Here we establish a domain-resolved framework for helical multilayer graphene that links supermoiré relaxation to low-energy electronic structure and valley topology. Real-space lattice calculations show that relaxation reconstructs the system into locally periodic single-moiré domains, enabling a local continuum description. Within each domain, downfolding the first-shell model yields effective Hamiltonians near the Dirac points that reveal how the low-energy spectrum decomposes into folded Dirac sectors. The resulting valley Chern topology is domain-dependent and includes gate-tunable responses, as independently corroborated by real-space lattice calculations. Our results identify folded Dirac sectors as the organizing principle of thicker helical graphene stacks, with local stacking families determining the band character and valley topology.
articles.summary_en: IOP Publishing researchers show that lattice relaxation in helical trilayer graphene forms locally periodic moiré domains with distinct valley Chern topology. The findings provide a framework for controlling low-energy electronic states in thicker graphene stacks, with potential relevance to advanced semiconductor devices.

articles.title_original: A Novel Sensitive and Stretchable TPU/MXene Film-Based Strain Sensor
articles.title_en: TPU/MXene Film Sensor Achieves 330% Stretch Range
articles.excerpt_original: The emergence of embodiment intelligence raises an immediate demand for high-performance strain sensors with adjustable large working ranges to enable precise deformation measurements. Herein, a high-performance strain sensor based on TPU/MXene composite films is fabricated via an ultrasonic anchoring strategy, and its sensing mechanism is investigated based on the piezoresistive effect. Benefiting from the synergistic sensing effect of the embedded conductive network constructed by ultrasonic anchoring and the reversible sliding behavior of surface conductive units, the proposed sensor successfully overcomes the narrow strain range limitation of conventional MXene-based strain sensors. The resulting TPU/MXene sensor delivers an ultra-wide sensing range of 0-330 % with a maximum gauge factor of 196.4. In the low-strain region (0-100 %), it exhibits reliable linearity (R² ≈ 0.99), and its signal output remains stable after 1000 tensile cycles. Besides, the optimized TPU/MXene sensor is demonstrated for bending‑deformation measurement on a silicone rod under different cyclic bending angles. This work provides a feasible preparation strategy for high-stretchability and high-sensitivity MXene-based flexible strain sensors, and shows great application potential in flexible deformation monitoring.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a stretchable TPU/MXene composite strain sensor fabricated using ultrasonic anchoring. The device provides a 0–330% sensing range, a maximum gauge factor of 196.4, and stable output over 1,000 tensile cycles, supporting flexible deformation monitoring.

articles.title_original: Breaking Water at Graphene Defects
articles.title_en: Water Dissociation at Graphene Defects Reveals New Interfacial Chemistry
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Water dissociation at solid surfaces underpins processes ranging from corrosion and catalysis to electrochemistry and photovoltaics. Defects often serve as reactive sites for dissociation, yet how solvation influences water dissociation at such sites remains poorly understood. Here, we use state-of-the-art machine-learned interatomic potentials to explore water dissociation at defective graphene–water interfaces. We show that solvation qualitatively changes the reaction mechanism at a graphene single vacancy (SV), opening pathways that are absent for an isolated water molecule. Whereas the gas-phase process proceeds via a single concerted channel, the solvated SV splits water through two competing pathways: a basic route forming SV–H andOH(aq)−, and an acidic route forming SV–OH and H3O(aq)+. These lower-barrier pathways produce distinct chemisorbed intermediates that enhance graphene–water adsorption. Accordingly, even a simple carbon vacancy gives rise to unexpectedly rich interfacial chemistry, coupling surface chemistry to interfacial charge and wettability, with implications for carbon functionalization and nanofluidic transport.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used machine-learned interatomic potentials to show that solvation changes water-dissociation pathways at graphene single vacancies, enabling basic and acidic mechanisms absent for isolated water. The findings clarify how defects influence graphene–water adsorption, charge, wettability, carbon functionalization and nanofluidic transport.

articles.title_original: Coherent MXene/metal interface builder
articles.title_en: Coherent MXene–Metal Interface Builder
articles.excerpt_original: Builds an MXene/metal interface in one orthogonal box, relaxes it with a MACE machine-learned potential and compares the built and relaxed structures.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a computational tool that constructs MXene–metal interfaces within an orthogonal simulation cell. The tool relaxes structures using a MACE machine-learned potential and compares initial and relaxed configurations.

articles.title_original: Machine-Learning-Accelerated Metallene Stabilization from High-Throughput Sandwich Modeling
articles.title_en: Machine Learning Maps Stable Metallene Sandwich Structures
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Metallenes have appealing properties, but stabilizing them in a monolayer phase poses synthesis challenges. A recent experiment showed that the van der Waals squeezing method can stabilize certain metallenes in a MoS2 sandwich. This pioneering work motivates systematic studies, but such studies are experimentally impractical, while first-principles modeling remains prohibitive. Here, using universal machine-learning interatomic potentials, we constructed 1620 metallene sandwich heterostructures containing 6 different sandwich layers and 45 metals. We performed phonon calculations, which revealed 1208 dynamically stable structures and narrowed them to 331 after structural filtering. We found that Se-based transition-metal dichalcogenides stabilize metallenes effectively. Specifically, hexagonal and buckled hexagonal crystal lattices exhibit the greatest stability. We further evaluated the thermal stability of selected heterostructures with density-functional-theory molecular dynamics simulations at room temperature. By uncovering the physical and chemical factors that govern metallenes stabilization, our results provide systematic insights to guide and accelerate synthesis for future applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used machine-learning interatomic potentials to screen 1,620 metallene sandwich heterostructures involving 45 metals and identified 331 structurally filtered candidates. The study finds Se-based transition-metal dichalcogenides and hexagonal or buckled hexagonal lattices particularly effective for stabilizing monolayer metallenes, guiding future synthesis.

articles.title_original: Cu-Anchored Keggin Ti–Oxo Cluster/Boron-Doped Carbon Nitride Heterojunction for CO2 Photoreduction
articles.title_en: Cu-Anchored Ti–Oxo/Carbon Nitride Heterojunction Enhances CO₂ Photoreduction
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Efficient and selective photocatalytic CO2 conversion in pure water requires both effective utilization of photogenerated charge carriers and well-defined catalytic active sites. Here, a Cu-functionalized Keggin-type titanium–oxo polyoxometalate/boron-doped carbon nitride photocatalyst (Cu–PT/BCN) was developed to integrate interfacial charge regulation with surface catalysis. Phosphate-centered PT clusters were grown in situ on two-dimensional BCN, followed by solvent-assisted ultrasonication to improve interfacial contact and cluster dispersion. The terminal {PO4} groups of the PT clusters were further used to selectively anchor atomically dispersed Cu species. Under UV–vis irradiation in pure water, the optimized Cu–PT/BCN exhibited markedly enhanced CO2 photoreduction activity, with CO2 conversion rates 7 and 30 times higher than those of BCN and pristine CN, respectively, while maintaining nearly 100% selectivity toward CO. Mechanistic studies revealed that charge transfer between BCN and PT follows a Z-scheme pathway, resulting in substantially improved separation of photogenerated charge carriers. The electrons retained on PT are subsequently transferred to Cu sites, which promote CO2 adsorption and activation and facilitate its selective reduction to CO. In situ microsecond transient absorption spectroscopy revealed an electron transfer efficiency of 80.5% under reaction conditions, while CO2 adsorption measurements and in situ Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy further confirmed enhanced CO2 adsorption and stabilization of the key COOH* intermediate. This work highlights metal-oxo clusters as versatile components for integrating charge regulation with catalytic-site engineering in photocatalytic CO2 reduction in pure water.
articles.summary_en: ACS researchers developed a copper-functionalized titanium–oxo/boron-doped carbon nitride photocatalyst that achieved CO₂ conversion rates 7 and 30 times higher than boron-doped and pristine carbon nitride, respectively, in pure water. The catalyst maintained nearly 100% selectivity for CO, with improved charge separation, CO₂ adsorption, and COOH* intermediate stabilization attributed to its Z-scheme architecture and atomically dispersed Cu sites.

articles.title_original: Superlattice Stabilization of the Topological Quantum Hall Ferromagnet in Graphene
articles.title_en: Superlattice potentials stabilize graphene’s topological quantum Hall ferromagnet
articles.excerpt_original: Competition between spin and valley orders makes graphene a versatile platform for engineering correlated topological phases in the quantum Hall regime. We show that a tunable superlattice potential reorganizes this competition, and stabilizes the ferromagnetic quantum Hall topological insulator at charge neutrality without requiring a large in-plane magnetic field or strong dielectric suppression of Coulomb interactions. The interaction anisotropies responsible for choosing between different competing states are first computed by a generalized renormalization group procedure that accounts for the superlattice potential. We find that the potential suppresses anisotropies that compete with spin-polarization. At the same time, the potential introduces dispersion which prefers a partly spin-polarized compensated semi-metal. Therefore, we carry out a self-consistent momentum-space Hartree-Fock computation with renormalized aniostropies to establish the regime of stability of the insulating spin-polarized ferromagnet. Finally, we verify that this ferromagnet is adiabatically connected to the quantum Hall ferromagnet, thereby confirming its topological character. Our results establish superlattice potentials as a means of controlling the phase diagram of interacting graphene and accessing its helical quantum Hall regime.
articles.summary_en: Researchers theoretically show that a tunable superlattice potential can stabilize a spin-polarized quantum Hall topological insulator in graphene at charge neutrality without requiring a large in-plane magnetic field. The findings identify superlattice engineering as a route to controlling correlated phases and accessing the helical quantum Hall regime.

articles.title_original: Twisting the pseudo–magnetic field lattice in periodically strained graphene
articles.title_en: Twisting Strain Lattices Suppresses Band Flattening in Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Periodic deformations flatten electronic bands of graphene which could host strongly correlated electrons similar to those observed in twisted graphene bilayers. The most spectacular effects of strong correlations like superconductivity or magnetism have however not yet been observed despite several experimental attempts. Here, we use tight-binding calculations to investigate the effect of twisting the periodic strain lattice with respect to the atomic lattice. We find that misaligning the two lattices kills the band flattening. We also report on the universal behavior of the band flattening by periodic strain which is controlled by a single parameter, a pseudo-magnetic field flux. Our study strongly suggests that controlling the twist of the strain lattice is essential to unlock the potential of periodic strains in graphene.
articles.summary_en: Tight-binding calculations show that misaligning a periodic strain lattice with graphene’s atomic lattice eliminates strain-induced electronic band flattening. The study identifies pseudo-magnetic field flux as the universal control parameter and highlights lattice-twist control as essential for realizing strongly correlated states.

articles.title_original: Nanomechanics of MXene Flakes at Gold Interfaces
articles.title_en: MXene Flakes Show High Interfacial Shear Stress at Gold Interfaces
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The demand for novel self-powering and sustainable electronics requires major efforts in identifying new advanced materials for nano-applications. MXenes have gathered attention due to their electronic and mechanical properties; however, their nanomechanical compliance against a metal-like interface is still not clearly identified. In this work, we employ atomic force microscopy to characterize the nanomechanical properties of a self-assembled thin flake of titanium carbide MXene (Ti3C2Tx) against a gold probe. The investigation returns an interfacial shear stress of 399 MPa and the observation of nano-wear localized in the center of the MXene flake. Nevertheless, MXene flakes retained their crystallinity in the tribofilms, as confirmed by transmission electron microscopy and electron energy loss spectroscopy. The outcomes of this work set the basis for the use of Ti3C2Tx in novel nano harvesting systems involving metal (e.g., Au) interfaces with large scope in nanoelectronics, wearable sensing, electric vehicles, and robotics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used atomic force microscopy to measure the nanomechanical behavior of Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene flakes against gold, recording 399 MPa interfacial shear stress and localized nano-wear. The flakes retained crystallinity, supporting potential use in nano-harvesting, wearable sensing, nanoelectronics, electric vehicles, and robotics.

articles.title_original: MXene untuk Sistem Pertahanan Indonesia: Tinjauan Literatur Sistematis tentang Aplikasi Radar dan Energi Pertahanan
articles.title_en: Review Assesses MXene for Indonesian Radar Absorption and Tactical Energy Storage
articles.excerpt_original: Material dua dimensi MXene (karbida/nitrida logam transisi) telah menarik perhatian signifikan dalam riset pertahanan karena kombinasi konduktivitas metalik, fleksibilitas mekanik, dan kemampuan fungsionalisasi permukaan. Tinjauan literatur sistematis ini mengkaji potensi MXene untuk aplikasi pertahanan Indonesia dengan fokus pada dua domain kritis: (1) material penyerap gelombang radar (Radar Absorbing Material, RAM) untuk teknologi siluman, dan (2) sistem penyimpanan energi taktis. Menggunakan metode PRISMA, kami mengidentifikasi dan menganalisis 15 artikel relevan yang diterbitkan antara 2021–2026 dari basis data Scopus, ScienceDirect, dan DOAJ. Analisis menunjukkan bahwa komposit MXene/Fe₃O₄ mencapai reflection loss (RL) hingga -57,3 dB pada ketebalan 1,9 mm, dengan effective absorption bandwidth (EAB) sekitar 2 GHz pada pita X. Sementara itu, komposit NiCoMoS/MXene menunjukkan EAB yang lebih lebar, yakni 8,2 GHz (9,8-18,0 GHz) dengan RL -56,4 dB pada ketebalan 2,61 mm. Untuk aplikasi energi, MXene menunjukkan retensi kapasitas pada suhu rendah hingga -60°C dan potensi sebagai elektroda superkapasitor berkapasitas tinggi (hingga 1040 F/cm³). Namun, tantangan stabilitas oksidasi, skalabilitas produksi, dan ketiadaan validasi prototipe masih menjadi hambatan utama. Kerangka konseptual diusulkan untuk mengintegrasikan penelitian material dengan kebutuhan strategis pertahanan nasional, menekankan pada validasi prototipe dan pengembangan rantai pasok domestik.
articles.summary_en: A systematic review identifies MXene composites with radar reflection loss up to −57.3 dB and reports potential for low-temperature energy storage and high-capacity supercapacitor electrodes. Oxidation stability, production scalability, and the lack of prototype validation remain key barriers to defense deployment.

articles.title_original: Polymer–Two-Dimensional Filler Composites for Hydrogen Barrier Materials: Transport Theory, Design Strategies, and Experimental Advances
articles.title_en: Review Examines Graphene-Enhanced Polymer Barriers for Hydrogen Systems
articles.excerpt_original: Hydrogen energy is widely regarded as one of the most promising pathways toward sustainable, low-carbon energy systems. However, hydrogen permeation remains a critical challenges for pipelines, storage vessels, and other hydrogen-related equipment. These issues not only reduce structural reliability but also raise significant safety concerns during long-term service. To mitigate hydrogen permeation, various hydrogen barrier materials, including metals, ceramics, and polymers, have been extensively investigated. Recently, incorporating two-dimensional (2D) materials used as fillers into polymer matrices has emerged as an effective strategy for enhancing hydrogen barrier performance by increasing diffusion tortuosity and suppressing hydrogen transport pathways. As a result, layered silicates (e.g., montmorillonite, MMT), graphene-based materials, MXenes (e.g., Ti3C2Tx), molybdenum disulfide (MoS2), hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN), and layered double hydroxides (LDHs) have attracted increasing attention for advanced hydrogen barrier applications. Despite rapid progress in polymer/2D filler composite barrier materials, which can be implemented as surface coatings, bulk liners, or free-standing films, enhancement of barrier properties through the optimization of nanosheet alignment, interfacial stability, oxidation resistance as well as scalable fabrication and long-term durability remain major challenges. Moreover, a mechanistic understanding of hydrogen transport and the structure-property relationships that determine barrier performance remains also insufficient, limiting their practical employment in hydrogen-energy systems.
