articles.title_original: Ion–Electron Coupling Transport in Semiconductor Nanotubes for Retinomorphic Vision
articles.title_en: CNT–ZnO Nanotube Device Enables Dual-Channel Retinomorphic Vision
articles.excerpt_original: A key limitation of current artificial visual systems lies in their single-channel signal transduction, which fundamentally departs from the parallel processing architecture of the biological retinas enabled by rod and cone cells. To bridge this gap, we developed a retinomorphic vision device by ion-electron coupling transport based on carbon nanotube (CNT)/zinc oxide (ZnO) heterostructured nanotubes. Upon optical stimuli, this device generates two distinct ionic and electronic current signals, effectively mimicking the parallel phototransduction pathways in biological vision. This dual-channel property enables efficient machine vision perception, achieving luminance adaptation and color discrimination accuracies of 96.5% and 98.2%, respectively. Furthermore, traffic-light-guided closed-loop navigation of a mobile vehicle in a real scene has verified its application potential in embodied intelligence. This "single device enabled, distinguishable dual-channel readouts" principle opens a new avenue toward artificial vision systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a carbon nanotube/zinc oxide heterostructured nanotube device that simultaneously produces ionic and electronic signals, mimicking parallel retinal phototransduction. The system demonstrated luminance adaptation, color discrimination, and traffic-light-guided vehicle navigation, indicating potential for machine vision and embodied intelligence.

articles.title_original: Graphene Concentration Effects in MQL-Assisted Ultrasonic Drilling of CFRP
articles.title_en: Graphene Nanofluid Reduces CFRP Drilling Forces and Heat
articles.excerpt_original: Drilling of carbon fiber-reinforced polymers is often accompanied by high cutting forces and heat accumulation, which negatively affect the quality of the final product. The thermo-mechanical correlation between cutting force and machining temperature during ultrasonic-assisted vibration drilling combined with minimum quantity lubrication using a graphene-enhanced biodegradable safflower oil nanofluid was investigated. Graphene as an additive was dispersed at concentrations of 0.25 mg/mL and 0.5 mg/mL with 1 wt.% oleic acid to ensure stable dispersion. Drilling experiments were conducted at spindle speeds of 1000, 3000, and 5000 min−1 and feed rates of 0.01, 0.02, and 0.03 mm/rev. The obtained hole walls were investigated using an optical microscope. The cutting force and the machining temperatures at the full tool–workpiece engagement stage were studied and compared with the results obtained by other authors. These measures allowed us to achieve a reduction in machining temperatures (T) by ~17.5%, in cutting forces (F) by 26.21–26.79%, and the roughness parameter Rz by 38.8% at the cutting conditions, where n = 5000 min−1 and f = 0.02 mm/rev at a graphene concentration (C) of 0.25 mg/mL.
articles.summary_en: Researchers investigated graphene-enhanced biodegradable safflower oil as a minimum-quantity lubricant for ultrasonic drilling of carbon-fiber-reinforced polymers. At an optimized graphene concentration, the process reduced machining temperature by about 17.5%, cutting force by up to 26.79%, and surface roughness by 38.8%.

articles.title_original: Formation of Two-dimensional Iron Oxide at the Graphene/SiC(0001) Interface
articles.title_en: Graphene-Encapsulated 2D Iron Oxide Formed at SiC Interface
articles.excerpt_original: Various elements are known to intercalate into the two-dimensional (2D) interface between graphene and a SiC substrate. By leveraging this intercalation phenomenon, we here demonstrate the fabrication of a crystalline 2D iron oxide at the graphene/SiC(0001) interface. Atomic-resolution electron microscopy revealed that the 2D iron oxide thus obtained is encapsulated by graphene and forms a sharp interface with the SiC substrate. Structural analysis and Mössbauer spectroscopy suggest that the 2D iron oxide exhibits a wüstite-like structure. This approach provides a new route for synthesizing 2D transition-metal oxides and enables the exploration of novel 2D materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated crystalline, wüstite-like two-dimensional iron oxide at the graphene/SiC(0001) interface through elemental intercalation. The graphene-encapsulated structure offers a route to synthesizing and studying novel two-dimensional transition-metal oxides.

articles.title_original: Kagome Flat Bands from Self-Assembled Water on Non-van der Waals 2D Materials
articles.title_en: Water Overlayers Create Kagome Flat Bands on 2D Materials
articles.excerpt_original: The properties of two-dimensional (2D) materials are governed not only by their intrinsic electronic structure but also in particular by their surface chemistry and interactions with the environment. The surfaces of non-van der Waals (non-vdW) 2D materials are intrinsically reactive and may require chemical stabilization under realistic experimental conditions. Here, we perform a systematic first-principles study of water passivation of non-vdW 2D materials and demonstrate that molecular water adsorption is energetically and dynamically favored for a wide range of systems. Rather than dissociating, water molecules frequently remain intact and form adsorbed ordered surface overlayers. These overlayers can adopt a kagome lattice geometry, leading to the emergence of flat electronic bands directly at the valence-band edge. Analysis of the electronic structure reveals a strong intermolecular coupling between neighboring water lone pairs within this kagome topology, while the locked molecular orientations simultaneously produce an electrostatically frustrated surface potential. These findings establish water not only as a stabilizing agent but also as an active element for electronic structure engineering of non-vdW 2D surfaces.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations indicate that intact water molecules can self-assemble into ordered kagome lattices on reactive non-van der Waals 2D materials. Intermolecular coupling and electrostatic frustration may enable water-mediated engineering of surface electronic structures.

articles.title_original: Kinetic Control of Symmetry-Broken Spin Architectures of Azafullerene on [10]Cycloparaphenylene Templates: From Frustrated 2D Lattices to Quasi-1D Chains
articles.title_en: Kinetic Control of Azafullerene Spin Architectures in Molecular Nanohoops
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Supramolecular host–guest complexation provides a powerful strategy for stabilizing organic radicals and organizing them into functional spin architectures. Here, we investigate the kinetic pathways for on-surface complexation of spin-1/2 azafullerene radicals (C59N•) within templated [10]cycloparaphenylene ([10]CPP) nanohoop monolayers on Au(111), revealing a strongly anisotropic energy landscape that governs radical migration and encapsulation. Migration of isolated C59N• along the [10]CPP rims proceeds via relatively low energy barriers (∼0.45 eV), leading to preferential confinement at the nanohoop periphery prior to azafullerene encapsulation. C59N• relocation to the global energy minimum at the [10]CPP center requires overcoming substantially higher barriers of at least ∼0.8 eV, with interfullerene interactions raising these barriers further. High C59N• mobility and relaxed lateral confinement at [10]CPP template edges also activate an alternative assembly pathway in which azafullerene intercalation induces in-plane exfoliation of [10]CPP lines from the 2D [10]CPP array, creating a reconstructed two-dimensional superlattice composed of alternating zigzag chains of azafullerenes and linear rows of encapsulated C59N•⊂[10]CPP complexes. This edge-driven reorganization gives rise to anisotropic lattices of encapsulated radicals with one-dimensional structural motifs. The control over the rich energy landscape of C59N•⊂[10]CPP complexation thus enables access not only to geometrically frustrated two-dimensional lattices but also to quasi-one-dimensional chain motifs of spin-1/2 carrying radicals within a single supramolecular platform.
articles.summary_en: Researchers mapped energy barriers governing azafullerene radical migration and encapsulation within cycloparaphenylene nanohoop templates. The approach enables controlled formation of frustrated two-dimensional lattices and quasi-one-dimensional spin-chain motifs, indicating potential relevance to molecular spin architectures.
